POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Fri, 16 Oct 2026 07:37:46 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.10 Deutsch-Französische Einigung zu „Made in Europe“ und Autoabgasen verzögert sich – SPD erhebt Einwände https://www.politico.eu/article/deutsch-franzoesische-einigung-zu-made-in-europe-und-autoabgasen-verzoegert-sich-spd-erhebt-einwaende/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 16 Oct 2026 07:35:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro-free&p=9175460 BRÜSSEL — Frankreich und Deutschland konnten sich am Donnerstag nicht auf einen gemeinsamen Standpunkt zum Geltungsbereich der künftigen „Made in Europe“-Vorschriften der Union sowie zu größerer Flexibilität bei der Reduzierung der CO2-Emissionen und zum Verbot von Verbrennungsmotoren ab 2035 einigen.

Der Entwurf des Gegenseitigkeitsabkommens, über den POLITICO erstmals im Juli berichtet hatte, stellt eine bedeutende Annäherung zwischen den beiden Ländern dar und sollte eigentlich in Kürze unterzeichnet werden. Am Donnerstagabend geriet das Abkommen jedoch ins Stocken, da der Koalitionspartner SPD Einwände erhob. Befürchtet wurde, dass wichtige Umweltziele gestrichen worden seien.

„Eine endgültige Einigung steht noch aus“, erklärte ein Sprecher der deutschen Bundesregierung.

Anfang dieser Woche hatte der französische Präsident Emmanuel Macron angedeutet, dass nun Deutschland am Zug sei. „Auf der anderen Seite des Rheins gibt es politische Zwänge, und ich respektiere die Koalitionsgespräche voll und ganz“, sagte Macron am Montag am Rande des Pariser Autosalons.

Gemäß den Bedingungen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens würde Deutschland strengere „Made in Europe“-Kriterien für den Automobilsektor im „Industrial Accelerator Act“ akzeptieren, auf die Frankreich gedrängt hat, im Gegenzug für eine Abschwächung des Verbots von Verbrennungsmotoren, einer der langfristigen Forderungen Berlins.

„Angesichts der erheblichen technologischen, wirtschaftlichen und geopolitischen Veränderungen seit der Einführung des bestehenden Rechtsrahmens sollte das Automobilpaket ein besseres Gleichgewicht zwischen Klimazielen, industrieller Wettbewerbsfähigkeit, technologischer Entwicklung und der Stärkung der europäischen Wertschöpfung herstellen“, schrieben die beiden Länder in einem POLITICO vorliegenden Vertragsentwurf.

„Auf der Grundlage der deutsch-französischen Ministerräte in den Jahren 2025 und 2026 schlagen Deutschland und Frankreich daher ein ausgewogenes Verhandlungspaket vor, das ehrgeizige CO2-Reduktionsziele mit zusätzlicher Flexibilität und gezielten Anreizen für die europäische Wertschöpfung verbindet“, heißt es in der Vereinbarung weiter.

Derzeit sieht das Ziel der EU vor, dass Unternehmen die Emissionen von Verbrennungsmotoren bis 2035 um 100 Prozent gegenüber dem Niveau von 2021 senken, wobei sie die Möglichkeit haben, sich durch Initiativen wie Ausgleichsmaßnahmen und Investitionen einen Spielraum von 10 Prozent bei den Emissionen zu „erwerben“.

Im Rahmen des vorgeschlagenen Abkommens wollen Frankreich und Deutschland das Ziel für 2035 auf 90 Prozent absenken und im Gegenzug für Investitionen in alternative Kraftstoffe einen zusätzlichen Spielraum von 10 Prozent einräumen (was insgesamt 80 Prozent ergibt).

Entscheidend für die Stahlhersteller und die linke SPD in Deutschland wäre, dass das deutsch-französische Abkommen die Investitionspflicht für „grünen Stahl“ abschaffen und damit einen wichtigen Anreiz beseitigen würde.

„Das zerstört den Leitmarkt für die Stahlindustrie“, erklärte ein Lobbyist der Branche gegenüber POLITICO unter der Bedingung der Anonymität, um über dieses heikle Thema sprechen zu können. Da der Vertragsentwurf keinen Druck auf die Automobilhersteller ausübe, „grünen Stahl“ zu beziehen, werde dieser dadurch zu einem „nice-to-have“-Extra, erklärte die Person.

Als Zugeständnis an Berlin wird im Vertragsentwurf betont, dass der sogenannte „Utility-Faktor“ – mit dem die Emissionen von Plug-in-Hybridfahrzeugen anhand des Verhältnisses zwischen der Nutzungshäufigkeit des Elektromotors und des Verbrennungsmotors berechnet wird – auf der Grundlage von Laborergebnissen und nicht, wie von der Kommission gefordert, anhand von Daten aus dem realen Fahrbetrieb ermittelt werden sollte. Diese Änderung wird den Automobilherstellern helfen, mehr Plug-in-Hybride zu verkaufen und gleichzeitig die übergeordneten Emissionsziele zu erreichen.

Als Gegenleistung für diese Emissionszugeständnisse schloss sich Deutschland der Forderung Frankreichs an, den Geltungsbereich der „Made in Europe“-Regelungen im Rahmen des „Industrial Accelerator Act“ der EU in Bezug auf den Automobilsektor einzuschränken.

Der Text gilt nur für die 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten und wird unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen auf das Vereinigte Königreich ausgeweitet.

Der EU-Industriekommissar Stéphane Séjourné erklärte am Dienstag gegenüber POLITICO, er unterstütze das Abkommen als Weg aus der Sackgasse, und fügte hinzu, dass das Vereinigte Königreich derzeit die Voraussetzungen für das Label „Made in Europe“ erfülle.

Die Vereinbarung könnte den Stillstand sowohl bei der CO₂-Verordnung als auch beim IAA beenden, bei denen Frankreich und Deutschland bisher auf gegensätzlichen Seiten standen. „Die Bestandteile dieses Gesamtpakets sollten so schnell wie möglich und gleichzeitig verabschiedet werden“, schrieben die beiden Länder.

Die britische Regierung begrüßte die mögliche Einbeziehung des Vereinigten Königreichs in die „Made in Europe“-Vorschriften für Kraftfahrzeuge.

„Dies ist ein deutsch-französischer Vorschlag, und es muss noch ein europäischer Prozess durchlaufen werden, aber sollte er bestätigt werden, begrüßen wir das Ziel, das Vereinigte Königreich in den ‚Industrial Accelerator Act‘ einzubeziehen – das wäre eine gute Nachricht für die britische Automobilindustrie sowie für die Arbeitsplätze und Investitionen, die sie im gesamten Vereinigten Königreich sichert“, erklärte ein Sprecher von Downing Street Nr. 10 in einer Stellungnahme.

Sollte der deutsch-französische Deal unterschrieben werden, muss es noch von den anderen EU-Mitgliedstaaten und vom Europäischen Parlament gebilligt werden, die derzeit über das „Industrial Accelerator Act“ und das Automobilpaket, einschließlich der Emissionsziele für Automobilhersteller, beraten.

]]> en Fonds publics détournés : pourquoi la Cour des comptes européenne pourrait avoir plus de mal à les repérer https://www.politico.eu/article/fonds-publics-detournes-pourquoi-la-cour-des-comptes-europeenne-pourrait-avoir-plus-de-mal-a-les-reperer/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 16 Oct 2026 07:07:57 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9161168 La volonté de la Commission européenne de rendre les milliards de l’UE plus réactifs aux crises à venir pourrait aussi les rendre plus exposés aux risques d’abus, avertit la Cour des comptes européenne.

Son président Tony Murphy alerte que les principaux piliers de la réforme du budget à long terme de l’UE, élaborée par la Commission, risquent de brouiller la vision des agents chargés de veiller à ce que les fonds publics soient dépensés comme prévu.

“Il nous est plus difficile de suivre l’argent”, a-t-il souligné. “On dit à l’Etat membre : ‘Voici une somme considérable, et vous faites en sorte que tout est en ordre.’ C’est en quelque sorte d’autocontrôle.”

Cet avertissement intervient alors que l’épineux débat du montant du budget 2028-2034 de l’UE est au menu du sommet des dirigeants européens à Bruxelles cette semaine, et que la Cour a constaté une augmentation des irrégularités dans l’utilisation des fonds publics.

Outre le montant total des moyens, se pose la question de leur répartition. Après un cycle budgétaire marqué par la pandémie, les guerres et les conséquences du changement climatique, la Commission souhaite rendre le prochain budget plus agile. Pour ce faire, elle prévoit d’en affecter environ la moitié — soit près de 1 000 milliards d’euros sur sept ans — à une enveloppe unique dans laquelle les pays pourront puiser pour remplir leurs objectifs dans des domaines comme l’immigration, l’agriculture ou le développement régional.

Ces fonds destinés à l’agriculture et au développement régional — souvent octroyés sous forme de subventions aux exploitations agricoles et aux projets locaux — sont depuis longtemps exposés à la fraude et aux détournements.

Selon Tony Murphy, accorder aux gouvernements nationaux une plus grande marge de manœuvre pour réorienter leurs dépenses rendrait le suivi de ces dernières encore plus difficile.

“Il y aura une certaine flexibilité, mais à quel prix ?”, a-t-il soulevé lors d’une interview. Une grande partie du contrôle dépendra des mesures de surveillance que chaque pays a déjà mises en place.

D’autant que les irrégularités dans l’utilisation des fonds du budget de l’UE sont en hausse. Les erreurs de versement se sont élevées à 5 milliards d’euros l’année dernière, selon le dernier rapport de la Cour des comptes européenne.

Dans le prochain budget de l’UE, il pourrait même s’avérer impossible d’estimer ce chiffre, a prévenu Tony Murphy, car les auditeurs de chaque pays ont des rôles et des méthodes de travail différents. “Année après année, nous avons constaté que le travail de ces autorités d’audit n’est pas entièrement fiable”, a renchéri son chef de cabinet, Wolfgang Stolz, lors de l’entretien.

Dans un communiqué, la Commission a défendu sa proposition, soulignant que les “principes fondamentaux” du système de contrôle actuel resteraient en vigueur. Les autorités nationales “fonctionnent bien”, a-t-elle affirmé, tout en précisant qu’elle se réservait le droit de demander aux Etats membres de “modifier le plan ou de mettre en place des mécanismes de correction si nécessaire”.

Des fonds mélangés aux budgets nationaux

L’une des innovations proposées par la Commission consiste à intégrer la politique agricole commune (PAC) — qui constituait jusqu’à présent une ligne budgétaire à part entière — dans un fonds gigantesque appelé plan de partenariat national et régional.

Tony Murphy a souligné qu’il ne prônait pas un modèle plutôt qu’un autre. Mais à mesure que les fonds européens s’intègrent de plus en plus aux budgets nationaux, il sera plus difficile pour Bruxelles de contrôler où va réellement son argent. La PAC est plus facile à contrôler lorsqu’“elle n’est pas mélangée à ce méli-mélo”, a estimé le président de la Cour des comptes européenne.

Les articles de presse sur des subventions agricoles versées pour de faux pâturages en Grèce ou sur des fonds destinés à soutenir le tourisme rural en Slovaquie qui financent de luxueuses villas pour les riches illustrent de manière frappante la difficulté de contrôler ces versements dans le cadre du système actuel.

Et le modèle sur lequel repose le nouveau système de dépenses — le fonds de relance post-Covid de l’UE — n’est pas de bon augure, a pointé Tony Murphy. Si les pays ont désormais plus de facilité à affecter les fonds là où ils sont nécessaires, les dépenses sont également devenues plus opaques. Les nouveaux plans nationaux ont été élaborés selon le même modèle.

Dans le cadre du système budgétaire actuel, la Cour des comptes européenne peut se rendre physiquement sur place dans une exploitation agricole bénéficiant de fonds européens. En revanche, dans le cadre du fonds de relance post-Covid, l’UE ne publie chaque année que la liste des 100 principaux bénéficiaires.

“Ce n’est pas très transparent. Je veux dire, où va réellement l’argent de l’UE ? C’est ça qui compte”, a insisté Tony Murphy. “On a un fonds qui regroupe différentes politiques publiques, avec des objectifs et des échéances complètement différents, des mécanismes de mise en œuvre différents et moins de prévisibilité.”

Here’s what’s going on. https://www.politico.eu/article/britain-lib-dem-liberal-democrat-ed-davey-meltdown/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 16 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9168716 LONDON — The Liberal Democrats used to watch their rivals indulge in messy factional squabbles with glee. Now they are scrambling to project an image of unity.

Britain’s third-largest Westminster group could hold significant power after the next election if no party wins a majority of MPs and Prime Minister Andy Burnham is casting around for a deal.

But for now, the focus is on weathering an internal storm in the centrist outfit. MPs rallied around their leader Ed Davey this week at a marathon four-hour meeting — held days after one of his frontbenchers resigned in an ill-fated attempt to oust the party chief.

The botched coup comes as the Liberal Democrats try to answer a more existential question: what are they actually for and how do they make an impact in Britain’s fragmented political landscape?

POLITICO’s Poll of Polls shows the Lib Dems coasting along. After getting 12.2% in the 2024 general election — and bagging a record 72 members of parliament as a result — the party has slipped down, polling between 9% and 11% since Andy Burnham became prime minister. 

POLITICO explains why Lib Dems are now openly discussing Davey’s future; how much danger he is in; and exactly how the man known for a cheery demeanor and eye-catching paddle-board stunts could be capsized.

1) Why is Davey’s future in the headlines?

The surprise resignation of the Lib Dems’ Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard a week ago triggered the latest round of soul-searching about the leader’s future — but the grumbling goes back a bit further.

Maynard’s resignation followed costly tax-cutting pledges from Davey at the party’s conference in September and came hot on the heels of sharp responses — including from 2024-intake Lib Dem MPs Tom Gordon and Vikki Slade — to the way Davey defended an existing guarantee on state pensions. Some MPs believe the party isn’t adequately representing younger voters by opposing changes to the so-called triple lock, now targeted for reform by Burnham.

The immediate threat looks to have receded. Maynard’s resignation has gone down badly among a host of colleagues.

One Lib Dem frontbencher — granted anonymity to speak about internal matters like others in this piece — said the “vast majority of us think it’s beyond ridiculous and are really angry.” A second frontbencher said it was “bang out of order” for colleagues to brief internal policy discussions to the press.

2) So he’s safe?

Not quite — fizzled plots like this have a habit of still bringing grumbling to the surface (just ask Theresa May)

There remains frustration among some MPs over Davey’s perceived failure to exploit a gap in British politics opened up by voters’ deep dislike of Keir Starmer’s Labour government after the 2024 general election.

YouGov’s Anthony Wells explains that the party was stagnant “during a period where the Starmer government came in, became extremely unpopular [and] lost a huge amount of support” that “didn’t go to them.”

He contrasted this with how the Lib Dems gained traction in the 2000s when the Labour government was in big trouble. The Lib Dems are normally good at grabbing “the low-hanging fruit of unpopular left-of-center governments.”

“They haven’t nailed their colors really firmly to any mast,” says Wells. “They have been something to all men — and it means they may have suffered in comparison to people like the Greens under [leader] Zack Polanski, who’ve been much clearer about what they stand for.” 

Removing a Lib Dem leader remains reasonably easy — though a crunch meeting of the parliamentary party on Tuesday suggests there currently aren’t enough MPs to actually trigger a ballot of no confidence, let alone win one. 

Eighteen MPs (25% of the parliamentary party) would need to push for a vote of no confidence to be held. An absolute majority — 36 MPs — would then have to vote no confidence in Davey for a leadership election to be triggered. 

Davey could stand in that leadership election if he could secure nominations from 10% of Lib Dem MPs and 200 members from at least 20 different local parties. 

Unlike in the Conservatives, where a leader cannot be challenged again for a year after they win a no-confidence vote, Davey would be given no such grace period if he survived — meaning another ballot could take place just months after he saw off a coup attempt.

3) What’s the view from Davey world?

The arguments in the leader’s favor appear to have won out — for now.

For one, he has a record of winning. Davey can point to having taken the party to its largest number of constituencies in its modern form by focusing on a fight-by-fight, seats-first strategy. The 2024 campaign prioritized targeted campaigning in specific areas, rather than seeking a higher national vote share that doesn’t translate to a high number of MPs.

Loyal allies have come out to bat for their embattled boss this week. Deputy Leader Daisy Cooper, seen as a possible future leadership contender, said there’s a “real sense that we need to come together as a group” to stop the Tories and Reform UK “from forming the most right-wing government in our history.”

Subtext: let’s not mess around and let our real enemies in.

A third frontbencher told POLITICO Davey doesn’t “just have the support of the parliamentary party — there clearly aren’t anything like enough MPs to trigger a vote of no confidence.” They said Davey changing his top team earlier this year by appointing James Holt as director of political strategy and Ruth Younger as chief of staff “just needs time to percolate.”

4) So can Davey just keep calm and carry on?

Maybe.

Wells believes the party doesn’t “necessarily need to do much” to hold its current crop of seats at the next election — and that a middle-of-the-road approach against flashier, potentially more divisive opponents — might actually work in its favor.

While “their brand may be less distinctive, it also means they’re more coalition-able,” Wells says. He points out that there’s already much less objection from Labour about working with the Lib Dems compared to the Greens, who Burnham this week threatened to can local power-sharing agreements with amid a row over anti-semitism.

“There is a strategic advantage to them in terms of not offending people, but there’s also a strategic weakness in not defining yourself very clearly,” he says.

Sam Francis contributed reporting.

]]> en Marine Le Pen’s EU dream is a nightmare for Brussels https://www.politico.eu/article/marine-le-pen-eu-dream-nightmare-brussels/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 16 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9168095 Welcome to Declassified, a weekly humor column.

The year is 2030 and French President Marine Le Pen’s sweeping overhaul of both her own country and the EU shows no sign of slowing down.

The Berlaymont, or the European Commission’s HQ, has been repurposed as the Ministry of National Sovereignty, except for the 13th floor —the current work base and living quarters of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen — which is now a cat cafe.

Other buildings in the EU Quarter of Brussels (or, as it’s now known, the 21st arrondissement) have not been so lucky. Most have been razed to the ground. Some have been occupied by disgruntled former EU staff, who are refusing to leave and have set up a working group to discuss a future roadmap that will feed into a discussion on how to bring back a European Union that Le Pen has largely destroyed.

Largely, but not completely. There is still an official EU office; the corner table in the branch of sandwich shop Exki near the Schuman roundabout (ironically, Le Pen used some of the money saved from dismantling the EU to finish the roundabout as planned). It is staffed 24/7 by Maroš Šefčovič, and he has a plentiful supply of leaflets.

Le Pen had more in store for the EU after her crushing 2027 presidential election win over Kylian Mbappé (who won a primary against Raphaël Glucksmann to be the unity centrist candidate, which was decided by who could do the most keepie-uppies).

The phrases “non-paper,” “stakeholder” and “trilogue” have been consigned to la poubelle de l’histoire. The European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee were closed down within weeks of Le Pen taking office, which shocked millions of Europeans who had no idea they ever existed. The European Parliament building is still there but is now occupied by a strange breed of zombie-like creatures wandering aimlessly through the corridors in search of something to do. No one can tell the difference.

Von der Leyen was, as Le Pen promised would happen, sent back to Germany where — in a somewhat unexpected move — she has become chancellor, succeeding Angela Merkel, who herself came out of retirement and orchestrated a coup to bring down current Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Anyway, back to 2026 and an EU reeling from a Le Pen speech in which she pledged to turn the Commission into a “secretariat” in the service of its member countries, and scrap some institutions altogether.

Le Pen gave her speech in Brussels on Wednesday and caught the train from Paris to Gare du Midi — if you haven’t been, imagine what the train station in Hell would look like, but with paninis. According to POLITICO’s railways correspondent, Miles Trackman, Le Pen was close to running into Michel Barnier, a former French prime minister (and who among us hasn’t been French prime minister?) and fervent Europhile who was spotted at the Paris station at the same time.

The question being asked in Brussels circles (and everything in Brussels goes around in circles) is: “Will Le Pen do a Meloni?” — as in, will she soften her stance if elected? The future of the Schuman roundabout may depend on it.

]]> en In Europe, the Trump shock factor is wearing off https://www.politico.eu/article/in-europe-the-us-donald-trump-shock-factor-is-wearing-off/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 16 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9170414 Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO.

Cast your mind back to last year, when European leaders scrambled back and forth across the Atlantic, seeking to patch up tattered relations between U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

After the Oval Office brawl where a scolded Zelenskyy pushed back against Trump and his vice president before being ejected from the White House, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer and French President Emmanuel Macron led the effort to engineer a call between the pair, during which the Ukrainian president expressed regret about the meeting — but fell short of apologizing.

Likewise, after Trump’s August summit in Alaska with Russia’s Vladimir Putin, Starmer and his top security adviser Jonathan Powell worked feverishly alongside other European leaders to rescue the broken relationship between Kyiv and Washington. They even came up with a ceasefire plan and got U.S. buy-in. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte also did some heavy lifting.

But this time, after Trump unveiled a controversial diesel deal with Russia and called — once again — for Zelenskyy to step down, the European reaction has been less febrile. Of course, they have offered Kyiv strong rhetorical support and unveiled more Russia sanctions, but there has been no frantic, panicky outreach effort to Trump to mediate a speedy repair.

Why not?

Because the Trump shock factor is wearing off, hazards Ukraine’s former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba. “The primary answer is that they have got used to him,” he told POLITICO. “They have all had an immunity shot, and they don’t feel as scared as they did last year.”

“Another reason is they’re drowning in their own problems,” he added. “And I think that first they feel they have to try to figure out how what Trump is doing will impact them — how big their bill will become as a result.”

European leaders are not scrambling like they did last year because Trump is “losing his leverage,” said Lia Quartapelle, an Italian lawmaker from the opposition Democratic Party who is vice chair of the parliament’s Foreign and European Affairs Committee. “We realize he cannot be trusted and we are on our own,” so there’s little point lobbying him.

According to the Financial Times, EU officials plan to urge Zelenskyy to tone down his increasingly sharp remarks about Trump, fearing they are only inflaming the situation. Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, is positioning himself as someone who can “lay the ground” for a reconciliation, he explained to the House of Commons Wednesday. 

Nonetheless, the calmer reaction to Trump’s maneuvers stands out, acknowledges Daniel Fried, a former senior U.S. diplomat who served as assistant secretary of state for European and Eurasian Affairs under U.S. President George W. Bush.

“The Europeans seem to have taken Trump’s measure,” Fried told POLITICO. “They want to avoid the worst. They want to mitigate the damage over the next two years while Trump is in office. They do work with people in the Trump administration with whom they can work. And there are such people.” 

Speaking from Warsaw, fresh from attending a recent security conference in the Polish capital, he said the Europeans understand now that much of what Trump does is performative and has a short life span — like the Russian diesel deal, which has a shelf life of two or three days, he said. “I’m not sure it’s going anywhere as it is utterly impractical and legally questionable, and it isn’t clear the Russians actually can supply the diesel,” he said. In other words, why get worked up about it?

Fried said in his conversations with European leaders and officials, he has detected increasing exasperation with the overall inconsistency of the American position: “Trump wants Europe to do more militarily, but it must buy American,” he said. “But we can’t sell to the Europeans because of our needs, so they will have to wait even though they can’t build it themselves. Nonetheless, they have to carry the load in Ukraine without us. That’s utterly inconsistent, and they are exasperated by it.” 

And they’re just tired of having Trump jerk them around, Fried added. “One thing they are trying to avoid is having Trump snap his fingers and they come flying. Because then it looks like they are at Trump’s beck and call and are his supplicants, and they don’t want to do that. Besides, if they fly out and talk him into something, how long will what he agreed to last?”  

Of course, the Europeans can also console themselves with the high chance of Trump reversing himself. “There is a pattern,” said Kuleba. “He launches a cavalry attack … and then retreats. That’s what we saw in February last year. That’s what we saw in November 2025. And that’s what we will see this time too.”

]]> en Budget showdown slips to November as Costa pushes for quick deal https://www.politico.eu/article/budget-showdown-november-antonio-costa-deal-european-council-summit/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Fri, 16 Oct 2026 00:56:56 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9173273 BRUSSELS — EU leaders will go back to the drawing board in November as they race to finalize a deal on the bloc’s next seven-year budget by the end of the year.

During the first day of a two-day summit in Brussels on Thursday, European Council President António Costa announced he was convening an additional gathering on Nov. 26 in a bid to overcome disagreements and lay the ground for a final deal in December. To bring the sides closer to an agreement, he will present new budget figures before the meeting, according to an EU official, who was granted anonymity to discuss the confidential planning.

Costa is pressing leaders to finalize negotiations by the end of the year — before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 threaten to derail the talks.

In a speech to the leaders, Costa warned that going past the end-of-year deadline will delay EU payments to farmers and researchers past Jan. 1, 2028, when the new budget is scheduled to come into force.

If leaders fail to reach a deal in December, the electoral calendar might push an agreement to May or even October 2027, Costa warned leaders in his concluding remarks, according to two EU diplomats briefed on the discussions.

Pressure on governments

Costa’s plan received a major boost on Thursday from French President Emmanuel Macron, who told fellow leaders that he won’t have a political mandate to sign a deal close to the French presidential elections in April 2027.

This is a major reversal for France, which has previously been unwilling to commit to the end-of-year deadline.

Macron’s words put more pressure on governments to advance the talks over the coming weeks — although some cast doubt on his good intentions.

“There are so many elections next year. [French far-right leader Marine] Le Pen herself [said] it’s undemocratic if we were now to agree,” said one EU diplomat.

Just hours before the leaders’ gathering, Le Pen renewed calls to halve France’s contributions to the EU budget if she wins the presidential elections next year.

She said that rushing the budget agreement before the French elections would be “a democratic scandal.”

The new frugal

Costa is stuck between messy domestic politics across Europe and hardening stances among the EU’s 27 leaders.

The so-called frugal EU countries pushing for major budget cuts — Germany, Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Denmark and Finland — have publicly said that an Irish proposal envisioning €159 billion cuts doesn’t go far enough.

On Thursday, the six hardliners were joined by Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, who joked in a press conference after the summit that “I’m married to a Dutch person so I’m very frugal also in my personal life.”

However, behind closed doors the budget hardliners employed a more conciliatory tone.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — the unofficial leader of the frugal camp — said that the Irish proposal has achieved progress despite reductions still being needed, said two EU diplomats briefed on the discussions.

He pointed to EU payouts to poorer regions, as opposed to farmer’s subsidies, as an avenue for cuts.

On the other side of the spectrum, Spanish Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez — who will try to cling on to power in an election on Nov. 29 — insisted that the budget is way too small.

“It is a distribution of misery,” he told fellow leaders during the discussions, according to the diplomats. He was joined by Italy’s right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni — an ideological foe on most issues, but an ally of sorts in the budget battle. She insisted that no further cuts to the budget will be accepted.

To bring sides together closer to a deal, Costa promised to advance progress on EU-wide taxes, or own resources, to finance the next seven-year budget and reduce national contributions.  

He will explore the European Parliament’s proposed taxes on crypto firms, online gambling and tech giants as well as a Greek idea to funnel future national sales of 6G mobile spectrum to the EU budget.

But given the level of opposition, getting EU countries to agree to any of these options will be no mean feat.

“It is time to be realistic and work on what is plausible and reasonable, instead of wishful thinking,” said another EU diplomat.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 15 Oct 2026 22:05:07 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Pressure mounts on EU leaders to strike a budget deal by December https://euobserver.com/243045/pressure-mounts-on-eu-leaders-to-strike-a-budget-deal-by-december/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 22:03:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243045 EU Council president Antonio Costa has been tasked to deliver a new compromise before EU leaders meet again on 26 November in Brussels, with the aim to strike a deal during the summit in December - after the Irish proposal failed to gain any support.]]> EU leaders met Thursday (15 October) for their first face-to-face talks on the 2028–2034 budget, killing the latest negotiation proposal put forward by Ireland.

Dublin, which holds the symbolic EU Council presidency, proposed cuts of up to €141bn from the long-term budget,  about eight percent less than the commission proposal. But it failed to make anybody happy, for different reasons. 

And now, EU Council president António Costa has been tasked to deliver a new compromise before EU leaders meet again on 26 November in Brussels, with the goal of striking a deal during the summit in December. 

An EU official said Costa deemed the deal in December as “essential,” urging EU capitals “to assume their responsibility”.

For Denmark, for example, it is important to have more funds for defence, borders, illegal migration, and competitiveness. “It will probably be as difficult as it was last time or even more difficult,” said Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen ahead of the meeting.

“We need unanimity in the Council. We are far from that unanimity,” also said German chancellor Friedrich Merz before meeting counterparts.

The EU is divided into two camps. The so-called Frugals (Germany, Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, and Sweden) want “several hundred billion” more to be cut, mostly from agriculture and cohesion funds, while 17 EU member states (self-named as Friends of Cohesion) criticise the savings. 

But time is of the essence to reach a deal this year, especially for French president Emmanuel Macron, who will be facing presidential elections in spring, and it is expected that a victory by far-right party National Rally leader Marine Le Pen would make it far harder to arrive at an EU deal. 

Le Pen has pledged that, if she comes to power, she will halve France’s contribution to the EU budget.

And Macron reportedly said in the room with EU leaders that from January onwards, there will be no political room for reaching an agreement.

]]> EU ‘open’ to curbs on imports of Chinese chemicals and machinery, after hybrid-car deal https://euobserver.com/243011/eu-open-to-curbs-on-imports-of-chinese-chemicals-and-machinery-after-hybrid-car-deal/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:59:29 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=243011 The European Commission “showed openness” to proposing trade "safeguards", a brake on imports that can cover entire sectors, such as chemicals and machinery. ]]> The EU is preparing to curb Chinese imports of chemicals and industrial machinery, following a successful deal with Beijing that capped hybrid car exports to the bloc.

The European Commission “showed openness” to proposing safeguards, referring to an emergency brake on imports that can cover entire sectors, an EU diplomat told EUobserver on Thursday (15 October).

And there was “broad support” for the idea among member states for the commission to proceed, the diplomat said.

Last week, trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič agreed with Beijing to cap imports of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 next year, which was less than half the amount expected this year.

He called the deal a “blueprint” for other sectors, a view which was publicly echoed by EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, also on Thursday. 

Under World Trade Organization (WTO) and EU rules, anti-dumping and anti-subsidy cases require Brussels to prove that Chinese firms sell at unfairly low prices or receive subsidies.

Safeguards do not need evidence under WTO rules, which allows them to be used as an emergency measure.

And the commission only has to show that a surge in imports is seriously harming European producers. 

“We like the idea, chemicals, machinery where there’s still a lot of Chinese overproduction needs to be managed,” said another EU diplomat.

The instrument had its limits: Safeguards have to apply to all countries, not just China, and can last no more than eight years.

Read more

EU leaders uniting on tougher China trade defence, but clash over carbon pricing rules

The EU rarely uses WTO safeguards, but did so on steel, also aimed at China, which expired in June, after reaching the eight-year limit, and which have since been replaced by a separate EU steel regime.

And the Centre for European Reform, a prominent think-tank in Brussels, previously suggested exempting the EU’s 76 free-trade partners from safeguards so that the measures fell mainly on China.

It was a legal moot point in the WTO if that was OK, but the EU has done something similar before. 

Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, and 10 other countries were left out of the steel safeguard, but using this tool to address Chinese imports was still seen as a temporary solution.

Before the end of the year, the EU commission aims to present diversification tools to reduce reliance on Chinese goods, as well as a mechanism to compensate companies hit by Chinese countermeasures.

And the package would include an instrument to shut Chinese companies out of the EU market if need be, in a measure first proposed in a Franco-German paper last week.

]]> How Slovakia’s Fico became Putin’s top ally inside the EU https://euobserver.com/242837/how-slovakias-fico-became-putins-top-ally-inside-the-eu/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 17:24:57 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242837 Slovak prime minister Robert Fico appears to have become Russia’s most prominent ally in the European Union, following the demise of Hungary's pro-Kremlin leader. ]]> Slovak prime minister Robert Fico appears to have become Russia’s most prominent ally in the European Union, following the demise of Hungary’s pro-Kremlin leader.

Juraj Blanár, Slovakia’s foreign minister, announced controversial plans to revive a joint committee with Russia back in August – just a day before the anniversary of the Soviets occupying Czechoslovakia in 1968.

His announcement also came before Fico headed off to meet his counterparts at a summit in Brussels on Thursday (15 October).

And “so that there are no surprises, on the 25th [of October] there will … be a meeting of the joint economic commission with the Russian Federation,” Fico told the European affairs committee in Slovakia’s parliament on Wednesday.

The central European leader announced the closer ties with his aggressive neighbour immediately after planning a trip to Lviv in Ukraine early next month.

But if Fico does actually go to Lviv, just over the border from Poland, it would be the deepest he has travelled in the war-torn country so far.

And while he has not visited Kyiv in three years since returning to power, Fico has made plenty of time to go to Moscow during this time.

Many factors point to Slovakia now openly supporting the Kremlin, even as Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilians intensify, killing dozens of people.

The Institute for European Security Studies (IESS), a Kyiv-based think tank, noted, in its analysis, that a recent statement by Slovak defence minister Robert Kaliňák did not consider Russia a threat, despite Russian intelligence services having been linked to attacks in Slovakia including, potentially, a drone attack on a manufacturer near Prešov.

The IESS also highlighted the renewed Slovak-Russian cooperation at the level of military attachés, with two Slovak military personnel sent to the Russian capital while a Russian officer went to Bratislava.

This swap of soldiers was promised by Fico to Putin when they met in the Kremlin on 9 May.

And to make matters worse, a Russian military attaché was captured on video handing cash to an associate of the Slovak fake news site Hlavné správy.

The Ukraine think-tank warned that Slovakia’s magnetism towards Russia should not be ignored.

“In the end, by lowering Nato’s guard and reopening the doors to Russian intelligence, Slovakia is doing exactly what Moscow needs: disabling the West’s defences from the inside out,” it said.

]]> Zelensky urges unity, more money for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia ahead of key summit with EU leaders https://euobserver.com/242983/zelensky-urges-unity-more-money-for-ukraine-and-sanctions-on-russia-ahead-of-key-summit-with-eu-leaders/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 16:47:27 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242983 Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Brussels with two main requests for his meeting with EU leaders on Friday: more funds for Kyiv for defence and more sanctions against Russia.]]> Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Brussels with two main requests for his meeting with EU leaders on Friday (16 October): more funds for Kyiv for defence and more sanctions against Russia. 

“All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed – more real pressure on Russia and more defence support for Ukraine,” he said on X.

“It is especially important now to act together to protect lives,” he added.

Zelensky’s plea comes days after US president Donald Trump announced a deal to bring Russian diesel to the US and global markets, raising questions about the consistency of Western efforts to restrict Russia’s energy revenues that are feeding the Kremlin war machine. 

EU leaders are expected to “regret” the Trump-Putin deal in their summit conclusions, where they also mention more financial, humanitarian and diplomatic support to Kyiv ahead of what many predict to be one of the most difficult winters for Ukraine.

Dutch PM Rob Jetten said the diesel deal was “not a good step”, adding that “Europe has to show that we are not only dependent on the US”.

But he also appealed directly to the US, calling for more support: “Do what is necessary to support the Ukrainians. They need not only sufficient weapons to defend Ukraine, but also the information they need to repel Russian attacks.”

Despite the diesel deal, Estonian PM Kristen Michal, whose country hosts a US military base, also said the US is still a “partner” of Europe in the war in Ukraine.

“We will see what happens in the midterm elections. But I will never give up trying to talk to and convince … our transatlantic partners that we are better off united than divided on this issue,” European Parliament president Roberta Metsola said during a press conference on Thursday after meeting EU leaders.

And in a warning to Moscow about Nato’s unity, US top military commander Alexus Grynkewich also said earlier this week in Warsaw that any “foolish” attack on the Nato alliance would be “utterly futile”.

Funding gap

In December 2025, EU leaders failed to agree to use over €210bn in Russian frozen funds sitting in Europe and instead decided to go for a €90bn loan, aimed at covering about two-thirds of Ukraine’s external financing needs. 

“The remaining third is the problem,” Tetiana Shevchuk, from the Kyiv-based Anti-Corruption Action Center, told EUobserver, referring to commitments by other countries like Canada and Japan coming only for 2026. “2027 is the real gap”.

The €90bn loan is split into €45bn for 2026 and 2027, but recent reports point to about a €23bn financial gap amid an expected Russian escalation ahead of the winter. 

Zelensky has asked Brussels to bring forward part of the loan to cover this gap in the defence ministry. But Brussels fears this advance “could unravel the compromise on gradual instalments and leave a hole later in 2027,” Shevchuk also said.

Another blow for Lőrinc Mészáros

Last Friday (9 October), prime minister Péter Magyar and Dávid Vitézy, minister for transport and investments, announced that the state was suspending implementation of one of Hungary’s largest rail projects – the Budapest southern circular railway, and will launch a new public procurement procedure.

The works had been carried out by V-Híd, the most profitable company of Lőrinc Mészáros, who became Hungary’s richest man during Viktor Orbán’s premiership.

However, the European Court of Auditors uncovered serious public-procurement irregularities: V-Híd may have colluded with the company that drafted the project plans and thus already possessed information at the time of the tender that its competitors did not have. Because of this, the European Court of Auditors would withdraw EU funding from the project.

The Hungarian government does not want to forfeit the EU money and make Hungarian taxpayers foot the bill for the costs of the project, which is why it is terminating the contract with Mészáros’s company and launching a new tender.

The Hungarian state had already taken away from Mészáros the right to operate a motorway section, and later also terminated the 35-year motorway concession.

Previously, one of his food-industry companies had EU funding already granted to it withdrawn, while his energy company was excluded from a call for proposals financed from the repatriated RRF funds.

On Monday (12 October), president András Baka nominated a former chief prosecutor, Péter Fejes, for the post of chief prosecutor. Fidesz, the Christian Democratic People’s Party (KDNP) and the far-right Mi Hazánk did not vote for the amendment; Magyar called this a disgrace.

    He told me he escaped from his village in Somalia in November 2024 when the Islamist armed group Al-Shabab attacked it.     Governments should also consider deferring repayment of the NGEU bonds, as the Draghi report suggested, especially if the own-resources reform falls short. It would protect priority spending when it is needed most.

    Sustained joint borrowing brings a bonus: more common safe assets in euros, which strengthens the euro’s international role. The demand is already there.

    Last month Piotr Serafin, the EU’s budget commissioner, flew to Seoul and Tokyo to meet investors. Asian buyers’ share of EU bond syndications has risen from 5 per cent to 9 per cent in the second half of 2025.

    Wobbles in US bond markets, which partly reflect doubts about America’s fiscal health, its reliability as a partner and the dollar’s safe-haven status, give the euro an opening.

    But it can only take it if EU governments put their own fiscal houses in order.

    Ongoing tensions in the French bond market provide a clear warning. Putting France’s finances on a sustainable path would do more than reassure markets about the euro. It would restore French debt as a safe euro asset.

    EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday in Brussels. Whatever they discuss (and later decide) on the budget, Europe should keep borrowing together, and in large amounts.

    The task now is to give that borrowing a coherent plan: a permanent framework, money set aside in advance and safeguards that cautious capitals can accept.

    ]]>         EU and Turkey explore closer trade ties to reduce dependence on China https://euobserver.com/242594/eu-and-turkey-explore-closer-trade-ties-to-reduce-dependence-on-china/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 11:09:55 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242594 The EU may not want Turkey as a member, but both sides can see the appeal of closer economic ties to reduce their dependencies on China.]]> Belgium’s foreign minister has called on the EU to deepen its economic, trade, and defence ties with Turkey, amid concerns from Ankara that it risks being shut out of the bloc’s new rules on industrial supply chains and multi-billion euro defence procurement scheme. 

    Speaking at a Turkey-EU business forum in Brussels on Tuesday (13 October), Belgian foreign minister Maxime Pévot said that European manufacturers were increasingly looking for reliable partners closer to home as they seek to reduce their reliance on Chinese inputs. 

    “We should make values of its proximity, particularly in sectors where Europe needs to reduce strategic dependencies,” he added. 

    “Our economic relationship should no longer be limited to buying and selling goods. We should also be developing, producing, and investing together,” he said. 

    For his part, following talks with Ankara’s trade minister, Ömer Bolat, EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič told reporters that the two sides had agreed on reforms to Turkey’s import control system to make the system easier for EU exporters to use and a mutual recognition pact on trusted traders.

    ]]>         Listen: When does a hybrid attack become an attack on Nato? https://euobserver.com/242601/listen-when-does-a-hybrid-attack-become-an-attack-on-nato/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 08:47:08 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242601 Two ships have been hit by drones in Bulgarian waters in the Black Sea on Monday. Several other ships have been targeted in recent weeks, at a time when Russia is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine.]]>

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    Two ships have been hit by drones in Bulgarian waters in the Black Sea on Monday. Several other ships have been targeted in recent weeks, at a time when Russia is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine.

    So, at what point does a hybrid attack become an attack on Nato? On Monday, two ships were hit by drones in the Bulgarian economic zone in the Black Sea.

    One of them sank, with 11 crew members missing. The second vessel, which belonged to Ukraine, was damaged but did not sink, and all 15 people on board were rescued.

    Read more

    Drone strikes on Black Sea cargo ships point to wider European arc of Russia hybrid threats

    A week earlier, two other cargo ships had been attacked by drones in the same area, killing 10 people. And on 5 October, a Turkish cargo ship carrying grain was sunk by drones shortly after leaving Ukraine.

    There is currently no evidence proving that Russia was behind these attacks, and Moscow has not claimed responsibility.

    But that did not stop Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev from summoning Russia’s ambassador. Radev said that, while there was no conclusive evidence, the outcome of these attacks clearly benefited Russia more than anyone else.

    Russia’s ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, said she had received no information from the Russian defence ministry about the attacks. She also suggested that they could have been provocations carried out by a third party.

    And that uncertainty is important, because it makes it much harder for Nato countries to decide when an incident should be treated as an attack.

    Read more

    [Interview] ‘Putin understands only strength’: EU envoy in Kyiv urges stronger air defences and hybrid-war response

    So how do Europeans cope with these attacks? We’ve already seen several Russian drones end up inside EU territory in recent months. And in some cases, they have been clearly identified.

    Take the Russian drone that crashed on a residential building in the Romanian city of Galați in May and injured two people. Or the two drones found at Leipzig airport in Germany this summer, charged with explosives. They were all identified as Russian.

    So far, however, the response has consisted mainly of diplomatic measures and political statements. Neither Bulgaria nor Germany has requested formal consultations under Article 4 of the Nato treaty.

    Article 4 allows a Nato member to ask for consultations when it believes its territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.

    Bulgarian Prime Minister Radev has spoken with Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte about the incidents, which are serious enough to be discussed at Nato level. But Bulgaria has not gone as far as triggering Article 4.

    One reason is precisely the ambiguity surrounding all these drone attacks: who is controlling them, whether they were deliberately sent into EU territory, and whether they were jammed or diverted.

    Read more

    Divided EU cyber defence faces real-life Russian and Chinese threats

    But if an attack were clearly attributed to Russia, how would Nato respond? That’s one of the questions currently being discussed within the alliance.

    On Monday, Nato’s top military commander, US General Alexus Grynkewich, said he did not believe a conflict between Russia and Nato was imminent or inevitable.

    But he also presented what Nato calls a “theory of victory”: a plan designed to ensure that the alliance could rapidly neutralise an enemy attacking one of its members.

    The strategy rests on several pillars. One is establishing clear red lines that an adversary should not cross. Another is investing in new military technologies, with drones playing a central role. And the third is maintaining the ability and readiness to fight at short notice.

    The idea is not only to be able to respond if a direct attack happens, but also to deter Russia from continuing what Nato describes as hybrid activities against its members.

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll</link>
      <description><p>Nearly 61% believe country is in recession and 65% of independents say economy is worse, according to new Harris poll</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>With the midterm elections less than three weeks away, key voting groups including independents, rural voters and even some Republicans are increasingly disenchanted with Donald Trump’s economy, according to an exclusive Harris poll for the Guardian.</p><p>The majority of those surveyed were pessimistic about the economy, with three-quarters of Americans saying they are concerned about a recession while 61% wrongly believe that the US is already experiencing one.       <title>US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/inflation-numbers-september</link>
      <description><p>Final inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under Trump</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/08/economy-midterm-elections-tell-us">Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections</a></p></li></ul><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/republicans">Republicans</a> are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/inflation">inflation</a> since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.</p><p>US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7%<strong> </strong>in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/trump-administration">Trump administration</a> over the cost of living.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/inflation-numbers-september">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”.       <description><p>When partners consider finances, when is it ‘my’ money, and when it is ‘our’ money? ]]>Joel Saget<![CDATA[What is the point of Ifac if the Coalition just ignores its warnings?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/what-is-the-point-of-ifac-if-the-coalition-just-ignores-its-warnings/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/16/what-is-the-point-of-ifac-if-the-coalition-just-ignores-its-warnings/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 04:15:00 +0000All bark and no bite. If you wanted to be cruel about Ireland’s so-called fiscal watchdog – that would be the obvious cliche to throw its way.

For years, the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council (Ifac) has advised successive ministers for finance to go easy on the spending increases and tax cuts, put away more money and account properly for the possibility of overruns.

Yet, time and again on budget day, much of the advice appears to be quietly ignored.

Take Budget 2027, for example.

The budgetary process now begins several months before the big day itself – with the Stability Programme Update in April, followed by the Summer Economic Statement (SES) in July. Between them, the two documents provide a good sense of what will be at the Government’s disposal later in the year.

In August, after having a good look at the SES, which outlined the broad parameters for the budget, Ifac said the economy did not need any budgetary support.

It said the economy continued to grow at a “remarkable pace” even when the distorting impact of the multinationals was stripped out of the official figures.

Casting his eye across the SES’s implied net spending growth, its chairman Seamus Coffey said the plans were “not appropriate” for an economy in such a strong position.

Ifac’s position was that if the Government continued down this road, then its policies would only add to an already worrying inflation outlook.

And what did the Government do?

Within hours of the budget’s publication, Ifac said it had put “the public finances on a worse trajectory by repeatedly breaking established spending limits and increasingly relying on high-risk corporation tax”.

Budget puts public finances on worse trajectory, watchdog warns

Coffey noted that, rather than heed the warnings, the Government was planning on spending €6 out of every €7 in corporation tax it collected.

The Government, as would be expected, defended the €8.7 billion in new measures. Minister for Finance Simon Harris had already defined the respective roles as he saw it.

“We don’t ignore their advice, but they’re not the Government,” he said.

So what is the continued point of having an institution set up in the wake of the 2008 crash to prevent a re-run of that calamity if modern-day governments choose not to take its advice?

Michael McMahon, a professor of macroeconomics, sat on the council for nearly seven years before serving as interim chairman between 2023 and 2024.

“When I joined, I thought we’d actually be advising the Government,” he says.

“That we’d go and meet the ministers involved and say, ‘This is a nonsensical policy; we think this would be better’. I thought it would be technocratic, geeky advice on the highest levels.”

Instead, McMahon quickly realised it was Ifac’s role to assess what was being proposed. “You could replace the word ‘advisory’ in Ifac’s name with ‘assessment’,” he says.

While chairman in 2023, McMahon added his voice to those of his predecessors, warning that the government risked “repeating Ireland’s past mistakes” with its upcoming budget. In particular, the tendency to breach its own spending rule had bothered the council members.

At the time, he said the State was over-reliant on windfall corporation tax revenues in the same way pre-crash governments had relied on property-related taxes.

How Budget 2027 will impact families: From renters to stay-at-home parents

McMahon also entertained the idea that, at some point in the future, Ifac could hit the “big red button” available to it and refuse to endorse budgetary forecasts. He said the council would be more likely to “wield big sticks” if the spending breaches were going to be repeated year after year.

Looking back, did his words and those of the other Ifac members have any impact?

“The question is not whether the government has always exactly complied with the letter of the recommendations,” he says.

“But rather, what would have happened with spending and tax decisions if an institution like the fiscal council was not endorsing the macro forecasts and criticising the decisions being made?”

McMahon says it is likely, in his view, that government spending would have been higher- and potentially riskier – had it not been for the role played by Ifac over a number of years.

During his time on the council, the government consistently ignored its own spending growth cap of 5 per cent annually, exceeding it each time.

However, the economist claims the cap may not have been introduced at all or, if it had, it would have been exceeded by an even greater margin had there been no independent oversight.

“It’s a very difficult thing to assess,” he says.

“I personally felt over the time I was there, it was a kind of slow beating of a drum of messages that were getting through. Questions were being asked in the media about growing spending at 6 and 7 per cent when their target was 5 per cent.”

McMahon also says it is his belief that the Future Ireland Fund (FIF) – the sovereign wealth fund into which the Government is investing 0.8 per cent of GDP annually – may not have come about had it not been for persistent calls for such a plan from Ifac.

“I think Ifac is useful; it has shifted the debate in Ireland. I don’t think we would have the FIF without it,” he says.

Ifac was established during the bailout years, when the country was picking up the pieces from an economic crash that pushed us into a three-year IMF-EU bailout.

Cut costs and abolish Ifac

Ireland had narrowed its tax base during the Celtic Tiger era and was badly caught out when the international banking crisis coincided with a collapse in house prices. An over-dependence on elements like stamp duty left public finances cruelly exposed.

Ifac, it appeared, was designed to remind policymakers that the same mistakes could not be repeated. Promoting fiscal responsibility seemed to be its overarching mission.

John Moran was secretary general at the Department of Finance between 2012 and 2014 when Ifac first got up and running. The terms of the bailout hung over the government, and the council was, at times, insistent on difficult medicine.

“We were in a tough position of trying to bring the budget back into order,” he says.

“There would have been moments of disagreement [with Ifac], where perhaps the political judgment of the government at the time was that they needed to do things that were seen as more politically palatable to keep the coalition together and keep the public onside.”

Moran says the economic landscape nowadays, in some ways, is comparable to the pre-crisis years.

“Today’s world is in a different position,” he says. “There are questions about how much extra spending you can do; that’s where the contrast lies [with the bailout years].

“We have some parallels between now and the situation before when we got into financial difficulties, with very concentrated tax sources.”

Budget 2027: Big business pays the bills as Coalition rolls the dice

The first chairman of Ifac was Prof John McHale.

He believes its importance lies in being able to publicise a counterpoint to government policy. Much of the time, he says, what Ifac is stating is not entirely different from what senior civil servants are telling ministers behind the scenes.

“It is different from [saying] it in public. In a way it helps the government – it helps balance the debate,” McHale says.

“You would never expect the government would take on what we would advise wholesale – it’s under huge political pressure. The council’s role was to take on a longer-term view. We were pulling in very different directions.”

So what was the relationship like between the government and Ifac?

“On the whole, it was good. Sometimes they were a little less forthcoming with information than the council would have liked, and it made our job harder,” he says.

That inability to always get the information it wants from civil servants could be solved, says McHale, by granting Ifac a statutory right. He points out that the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has again recently called for this.

That report also highlighted the relative lack of resources available to the council.

Applauding its ability to shape the media narrative here, the OECD said the body “punches above its weight”. It said Ifac ranked highly among similar bodies in other countries and had an ability to “generate influence despite limited resources”.

While winning plaudits from external reviewers, some politicians have eyed Ifac with a little suspicion over the years.

At a time when Ireland was crying out for public investment, particularly in housing, it has been accused of sometimes offering a narrow and needlessly cautious prescription. Yes, the argument went, the economy is doing well, but there are huge gaps where more money should also be spent.

How can runaway spending in the health service be reined in?

Sinn Féin’s spokesman on finance, Pearse Doherty, says there could be “question marks” over some of Ifac’s warnings down through the years, which were perhaps “too conservative”.

“If we look back at Ifac’s recommendations – and they have gone unheeded by the government in the past – the economy has still continued to grow and continued to have surpluses,” he says.

However, he says the council has played an important role over recent budgets in highlighting consistent spending overruns.

“Ifac have focused – and I think they have been misrepresented in my own view – on the government’s unplanned spending,” he says.

“It undermines the budget day process. You have a situation where the government announces X amount of spending on budget day, but by the end of the year, that has gone up due to unplanned measures.”

Doherty says he doesn’t know what Ifac would have to say about his party’s budget plans. But he believes it would be in line with Ifac’s current thinking on how the funding of extra spending should be done through the raising of additional tax revenues.

“The big difference between us and the Government is that we would increase capital expenditure,” he says. “I’m not sure what view they (Ifac) would take in relation to that.”

The other question that gets thrown at the “watchdog” is whether it is still needed, given that bodies such as the Central Bank of Ireland and the ESRI frequently offer similar criticisms of budgetary policy. The groupthink that prevailed in the pre-crisis period, so the argument goes, is no longer a problem.

With so much cash sloshing around, why is there a housing crisis?

“It is certainly true that there is a lot of common ground between the ESRI, the council and the Central Bank,” says McHale.

“It makes a difference when you have a body that has a statutory role in assessing these things. The Government has to respond to the council’s report; that is what really makes it stand out.”

McHale, though no longer part of Ifac, believes that budgetary policy is in a “reasonable place”. Despite criticisms around the nature of windfall taxes, he says it remains important that the Government is still running surpluses, though he’d like these to be higher.

This would be wise, he says, “given the underlying risks we face”.

McMahon says Ifac is more about “shaping thinking than shaping policies” and it fits the role of a “town crier”.

“We would all love 10 per cent growth a year, and everyone get free cookies,” he says.

“But we all know the pain that comes from reckless fiscal policy, and there is generally more pain than there is fun on the upside.”

]]><![CDATA[Netflix turns to former Disney executive to revive growth]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/wires/bloomberg/2026/10/16/netflix-turns-to-former-disney-executive-to-revive-growth/https://www.irishtimes.com/wires/bloomberg/2026/10/16/netflix-turns-to-former-disney-executive-to-revive-growth/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 06:28:10 +0000Netflix is replacing its chief creative officer with a veteran TV and film executive Peter Rice as the streaming giant looks to reinvigorate growth amid a slowdown in viewers and revenue.

Rice previously served as chairman of general entertainment at Walt Disney Company and, before that, as president of 21st Century Fox.

He will assume the new role later this month, with a broad mandate, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film and live events across all regions.

Rice replaces Bela Bajaria, who had worked at Netflix for 10 years and come to be the public face of the company’s content strategy.

Bajaria was credited with broadening Netflix’s entertainment offerings by expanding its unscripted portfolio and striking a deal with the TKO Group Holdings to bring the WWE’s weekly wrestling show, Raw, to the streaming service. She memorably described the ideal Netflix program as a “gourmet cheeseburger” — something combines quality and broad appeal.

The executive shakeup, coupled with Wednesday’s layoffs of some 1,000 workers or 6 per cent of its staff, are a sign that the streaming industry leader is trying to reinvent itself after seeing its audience growth slow and its stock price tumble.

The service has grown to more than 325 million subscribers globally. But it has evolved from a producer of “prestige TV” shows like House of Cards and The Crown to a broader entertainment source, competing with everything from sports channels to YouTube videos, and doing so on a global basis.

In moving Rice into the role, Netflix’s senior leadership see an opportunity to install an executive with deep relationships to Hollywood talent and experience running a broad portfolio of channels and streaming services. At Fox and later at Disney, he supervised a TV lineup that included hits from The Simpsons to Modern Family.

Recent Netflix shows have seen their audiences decline in their second seasons. The service saw its Emmy Awards wins fall to a 10-year low in 2026. The stock has lost about 23 per cent of its value this year.

Netflix co-chief executive Ted Sarandos, speaking at the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last month, acknowledged that the company isn’t growing as fast as he would like.

While the company has been expanding into live sports and podcasts, the vast majority of Netflix’s roughly $20 billion programming budget goes to films, TV shows and video games.

“Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry,” Sarandos said in a statement Thursday. “He understands what makes stories resonate, and he’s spent his career helping talent do the best work of their lives.” – Bloomberg

]]>Dara Mac Donaill<![CDATA[The CSO, MyHome or Daft: who’s right on house prices?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/16/the-cso-myhome-or-daft-whos-right-on-house-prices/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/10/16/the-cso-myhome-or-daft-whos-right-on-house-prices/Fri, 16 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000In the lead-up to the property crash of 2008 there was – let’s just say – unease about the number of estate agencies publishing what you might call self-interested house-price surveys.

Critics said their reports, and some of the commentary that went with them, were deliberately amplifying positive trends to encourage transactions.

When things began to sour, the “endless growth” narrative around Irish property gave way to the soft-landing narrative: “Okay, things have got a little frothy, there will be a modest correction, but the market is still structurally sound.”

When that thesis collapsed, and Ireland suffered the biggest peak-to-trough property crash of any country, property-price surveys (industry ones) were blamed for exacerbating the problem.

The task of producing an accurate data series on property price trends was given to the Central Statistics Office (CSO). In 2011 the agency began producing the Residential Property Price Index (RPPI), which remains the State’s official indicator of price trends.

A decade and a half later the industry barometers have crept back into the mix, led by the State’s two main property portals: MyHome and Daft. (MyHome is owned by The Irish Times Group).

While both companies’ quarterly reports are viewed as highly credible, they contain structural biases. Foremost, they base their quarterly surveys on asking prices rather than sold prices. In a sellers’ market, where buyers can get into bidding wars, these metrics can underestimate prices. The reverse is true when the market turns.

“From 2024 through to the spring of this year, transaction prices rose faster than list prices, and buyers typically paid well over the list price,” author of the Daft report Ronan Lyons said in the company’s latest survey.

Irish house prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit a price ceiling

“That has now reversed. Nationally, list prices are rising over two percentage points faster than transaction prices, the widest gap since 2023,” he said.

While Daft commands a larger market share of listings nationally, Daft and MyHome are said to be neck and neck (in terms of the listings market) in Dublin and Leinster, with most listings on both portals coming from estate agents.

Are we turning a corner on housing?

There are also quarterly surveys from Sherry Fitzgerald, Douglas Newman Good (DNG) and the Real Estate Alliance (REA), which use different methodologies.

At the moment they all tell the same story: house prices are still rising but at a slower pace than before because of a combination of affordability pressures linked to higher inflation, higher borrowing costs, enhanced supply and the uncertain economic outlook.

Further interest rate hikes and no resolution to the Iran crisis are likely to accelerate this trend.

Daft’s snapshot of the market in the third quarter put headline annualised inflation (for asking prices) at 3 per cent, half the level that it was a year ago. In Dublin the rate of price growth was estimated at 2.7 per cent.

MyHome’s equivalent report, published on Tuesday this week, put asking price inflation at 3.9 per cent and at 2.1 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s official numbers, also published on Tuesday, put inflation (for prices paid) at 5.1 per cent in August and at 3.9 per cent in Dublin.

The CSO’s numbers are based on stamp duty data from Revenue and reflect transactions that took place at least two months ago, so there’s a lag. Because they are based on asking prices, the MyHome and Daft reports provide more of an instant snapshot of which way the market is turning.

The CSO estimates the average price paid for a property nationally in the 12 months to August was €442,512, while in Dublin it was €598,677.

For MyHome, the average price nationally was €461,084 and €585,132 in Dublin. For Daft, the figures were €445,000 and €635,000.

The CSO and MyHome use median (middle value) prices in their reports instead of average prices.

With any property price survey, there is a need to distinguish between quality-adjusted price changes [those controlled for location, property type, new versus old homes, etc] and pure price inflation.

The CSO breaks its figures down by Eircode, which reveals significant price disparities not just between Dublin and the rest of the State but also within the capital itself.

Take, for example, the difference between Dublin 6, which covers Ranelagh and Rathgar, where the average price paid for properties last year was just shy of €1 million (€995,709), making it the most expensive Eircode in the State, and Dublin 10, which includes Ballyfermot and Cherry Orchard, where the average price was €333,391.

Irish house price inflation slows as affordability constraints bite

According to MyHome, house prices in Tuam in Galway have risen by 10.2 per cent in 2026 while prices in Kilkee in Clare have slumped by almost 13 per cent.

So while the CSO, MyHome and Daft capture the general direction of travel, they can differ significantly because of the disparity between asking prices and actual sale prices.

Put another way, MyHome and Daft measure what sellers want; the CSO measures what buyers actually pay.
