]]>Provision<![CDATA[The rich are getting richer, so why no wealth tax?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/the-rich-are-getting-richer-so-why-no-wealth-tax/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/15/the-rich-are-getting-richer-so-why-no-wealth-tax/Thu, 15 Oct 2026 12:03:13 +0000Around the world, the rich are getting richer, with soaring stock markets and other asset values lining their pockets. So why – in most countries – is there no wealth tax?

True, most tax systems do tax wealth in specific ways, such as charges on property or capital gains. But straight-up wealth taxes – an annual charge on the value of the assets held – are rare.

But with exchequers worldwide searching for cash, taxing wealth is coming back on to the agenda. A new report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) crunches the numbers and outlines the key choices facing Irish policymakers.

It shows there is a lot of wealth in Ireland that could be taxed, but raising a significant amount of money requires big political decisions.

For Ireland, as for other countries, the choice is whether a wealth tax would be for show – a political signal that the wealthiest should pay a bit more – or for dough, in other words to raise a significant amount of money for the exchequer.

Higher wealth – fewer wealth taxes

One of the peculiarities of recent years is that although the wealth of the billionaire class has risen worldwide, the number of countries with wealth taxes has shrunk.

The ESRI report points out that 12 European countries levied an annual tax on net wealth in 1990 compared with only Norway, Spain and Switzerland last year.

Low revenue yields, administrative challenges and concerns that capital would move to other countries are among the reasons cited for countries abandoning the taxes.

France abolished its wealth tax in 2018, citing fears of wealth moving out of the country, and replaced it with a tax on real estate worldwide assets valued at more than €1.3 million. Despite rising wealth, the key message is that full-scale wealth taxes are not easy to design and implement.

Wealth in Ireland

Household wealth in Ireland, as measured by the Central Statistics Office household finance and consumption survey in 2023, was €927 billion, about two-and-a-half-times higher than a decade earlier.

That is an average (median) net wealth of just under €256,000 per household, with the family home the main asset for the vast majority. Where a mortgage is still outstanding, this is subtracted from the net wealth figures.

The story of Irish assets over the past decade can be told in a few headlines – rising house prices are the key factor, followed by lower household debt as the Celtic Tiger loans are paid down and a rise in business assets among the better off.

The top 10 per cent still controls close to 50 per cent of wealth. It is worth noting, also, that separate Central Bank of Ireland data, which showed wealth at just over €1 billion early 2023 – a bit higher than the CSO – estimated it at being more than €1.42 billion in the first quarter of this year.

Taxing questions

Assets are taxed in Ireland via a few routes, notably capital gains tax and capital acquisitions tax on inheritance and gifts.

However, even if you add the amounts collected via these taxes to stamp duty and local property tax – which operates more like a charge – the total revenue comes to less than €6 billion in 2025 out of total tax revenue of more than €105 billion. Could a wealth tax increase the revenue significantly?

Well, it depends. The key insight from the ESRI paper was that if an Irish wealth tax was going to raise significant money, then it would have to have a wide base – in other words most assets would have to be included. If this happened, then even if the tax kicked in at relatively high wealth levels, significant sums could be raised.

The political problem is that a broad base takes in areas such as businesses, farms and the family home. If all wealth in the State were taxed at 1 per cent, the yield would be €9.3 billion based on the 2023 figures and probably more than €10 billion now. This is not a realistic scenario, but it provides a kind of benchmark.

The researchers go through a range of scenarios, with the widest possible tax base, one excluding the family home and a narrow definition including mainly financial assets and investment property. Cut-off points above which wealth would be taxed range from €250,000 to €2 million, with these figures doubled for a married couple. In all cases the tax rate is 1 per cent and pensions are excluded.

Three lessons

The first – and most striking – lesson is the importance of the range of assets covered. Exempting the family home, businesses and farms cuts the pot significantly.

At a threshold of €500,000 for example – which would be €1 million for a married couple – a narrow base just including financial assets and other investments would raise less than €450 million annually, while one including all assets would raise close to €3 billion.

The second lesson is not surprising: it is that as the threshold lowers for the wealth level where the tax kicks in, the numbers rise sharply.

At the €500,000 threshold, 4.5 per cent of households have to pay. At the lowest one, €250,000, it rises to more than a third. But the share of total national wealth rises less sharply – from 19 per cent to 32 per cent – as the amount of assets held per household falls sharply at lower levels.

The third lesson reflects the importance of the family home as the source of wealth for middle and higher earners. The main residence is only a small portion of wealth at the very highest level – where households typically own businesses or have significant financial asset. For middle Ireland, the family home is the key asset.

For a wealth tax covering everyone with assets over €250,000, exempting the family home would cut the annual tax take from €4.5 billion to €2.6 billion.

Who pays?

The profile of those who pay depends crucially on the rules set. The wealthiest top 10 per cent will always be hit hardest, but a key political decision would be where to draw the line. Too high and you limit the revenue raised. Too low and it ends up as a family home tax on middle earners.

The fact that there are wealthy people with relatively low incomes is another complication.

Overall, an Irish wealth tax would mainly hit middle-aged and older property owners – those aged 55 years of age plus would pay about two-thirds of the tax under most scenarios. If the base of the tax is narrow – excluding the family home – then those aged 65 or more would be in the firing line as those hold higher investments in savings and other financial assets.

They would typically paying close to half or more of the total tax, depending on the rules. On the flip side, younger renters hold hardly any wealth, so would pay little tax.

The bottom line

The report underlines that a wealth tax could raise a significant sum in revenue, but only if it covered a broad base of wealth.

This brings politically sensitive areas of business and farm wealth and the family home into the picture – all advantaged by the Irish tax system at present. An alternative, as recommended by the Commission on Tax and Welfare in 2023, is to increase existing taxes on wealth rather that introducing a separate new wealth tax.

But there is no easy decisions either here for Irish politicians – do they, for example, end the favourable inheritance rules for businesses and farms? Or hike local property tax?

None of these things will happen for as long as there is a budget surplus. But with the Irish Fiscal Advisory Council warning that more revenue will be needed in the years ahead to meet the costs of an ageing population and climate change, sooner or later Irish policymakers will have to consider where it comes from.

Sinn Féin has called for a study on a wealth tax and recommended hikes on capital taxes and pensions. Labour’s alternative budget also calls for a hike in a range of capital taxes, including capital gains tax and the capital acquisitions tax.

The Social Democrats want to tax the “super-wealthy”, likely only to work as part of an international drive in this area, while People Before Profit also want to “tax the multi-millionaires.”

But more taxes on wealth are now creeping on to the Irish political agenda. The comfortable classes are in the firing line – even if they don’t realise it yet.

Then, a few days ago, he made a deal with Vladimir Putin to release Russian diesel on global markets, in violation of sanctions imposed after Putin’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.

Trump also told Kyiv to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and threatened to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine and access to US-made weapons.

This “deal” is both foolish and wicked: foolish, because it is too small to lower diesel prices significantly, and wicked, because it is prepared to sacrifice a country that is struggling heroically to be free from tyranny.

Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.

Thus, the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest World Economic Outlook (WEO) starts with the following comment from Silvana Tenreyro, the new economic counsellor: “In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events.”

Current US policymaking is not just reckless and immoral. It is also one of the causes of the world’s unpredictability.

Yet all but one of these shocks, the exception being the pandemic, are man-made, or perhaps “strongman-made”. The others are the war in Ukraine, the tariff war and the war in the Middle East. Putin launched the first of these in 2022. Trump, of course, began the other two.

These shocks have, as Tenreyro says, “tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets and governments. Individually, each of these big developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary.”

Yet, remarkably, the WEO’s forecasts for growth this year and next, at 3.1 and 3.4 per cent respectively, are “broadly unchanged from April”, despite more persistent energy disruption than was then expected.

Global inflation is, however, expected to hit 4.7 per cent this year, as a result of higher commodity prices, and 4.1 per cent in 2027. But, happily, “the pass-through to core inflation is expected to be limited”.

The explanations for this resilience are familiar. They include adjustment of exports and imports away from direct trade between the US and China. More recently, however, the dominant factors have been the flexibility of the global energy economy, discussed here last week, and the investment boom triggered by artificial intelligence (AI).

Yet neither is guaranteed to last. As Nick Butler points out, stocks of crude and products are low after six months of drawdowns. Moreover, “product exports of diesel and jet fuel [from the Gulf] remain minimal”. Also at risk are supplies of naphtha, urea and liquefied natural gas (the latter of special importance to Europe).

The AI investment boom also concentrates risk. Even if AI itself works out, the level of investment is likely to stop growing, if not decline, at some point. Moreover, AI might not work out financially on the hoped-for scale at all.

Other fragilities are evident, notably the fiscal positions. Despite the big post-pandemic rise in real and nominal interest rates, most large economies continue to run significant primary fiscal deficits (before interest payments).

It would help if the shocks stopped, too. Alas, given our leaders, I would not bet on that.

The US position stands out, with a forecast primary fiscal deficit of 4.8 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, a share of T-bill issuance in gross borrowing at 58 per cent and an average maturity of a mere 5.9 years.

The WEO rightly emphasises the importance of rebuilding fiscal space. The good news is that, in today’s circumstances, the negative impact of structural fiscal tightening is likely to be offset by lower real and nominal interest rates. But redressing global current accounts imbalances will also be essential. That must, at last, involve China.

Ireland is richer and spending more than 30 years ago but is it making us happy?

The WEO emphasises other downside risks, including a worsening of the ongoing wars, (probably AI-enhanced) cyber threats and climate catastrophes.

Neither a stock market crash nor a collapse in AI-related investment can be ruled out, should returns on AI disappoint. Upside economic risks include still faster progress with AI technology, though that could also inflict devastating social consequences.

Another plausible upside is an accelerated energy transition, as recent events underline the unreliability of fossil fuels. Given their physical location, these are bound to remain so for many countries.

John FitzGerald: Budget reversal of policy on tackling climate change was a mistake

The WEO notes that the ability to exploit AI and meet energy needs reliably will be crucial for growth prospects. Sadly, the world’s poorest countries are particularly vulnerable in both respects. Thus, the WEO rightly fears that their living standards are likely to fall still farther behind those in richer countries.

It would be good to believe the world will become less prone to shocks. But it will probably not do so. The best response is to strengthen fundamentals, notably economic flexibility and dynamism, together with energy resilience. In this context, as the WEO notes, it is essential to make support for people vulnerable to shocks targeted and temporary.

The time for throwing public money around freely has come to an end. It would help if the shocks stopped, too. Alas, given our leaders, I would not bet on that. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

The boss who believed in you and gave you opportunities or the manager who thwarted and belittled you at every turn?

The managerial personality traits and behaviours we observe early in our careers often shape our own management style later. If we liked a boss, we might try to emulate what they did well while avoiding the more negative behaviours of someone we considered a bad leader or a toxic colleague.

In Ireland, many people who are promoted to manager never receive any training on how to manage or even know what good looks like. On a Monday, they’re a colleague and on Tuesday, they’re the boss.

To figure out how to behave as a manager, they might do a little detective work to determine what style is preferred at their company. If Mary was promoted for hitting her targets every month – regardless of staff burnout levels – then that might be someone they choose as a role model.

Or they might look higher up the ladder to the chief executive. If that person is a strong communicator who motivates the team with a clear vision and regular updates then they might choose to focus on developing these behaviours first.

Organisations that value sustainable growth and efficiency should never leave managerial expectations to chance. The cost of this oversight is high when it comes to employee engagement, turnover and productivity.

People don’t leave jobs, they leave bad managers.

Managerial skills continue to be a gap in Ireland, with 61 per cent of HR professionals surveyed identifying insufficient line manager capability and capacity as the top constraint, according to the CIPD Ireland’s HR Practices in Ireland 2026.

According to Gallup, half of resigning employees cite their manager as the reason they’re leaving. That’s not surprising considering that so much of your compensation, growth opportunities and motivation come from interactions with your manager. This relationship – good or bad – correlates directly with employee engagement.

Employees who leave because of their manager say poor communication, lack of recognition, micromanagement, favouritism and unfairness are the top reasons the relationship breaks down. Companies spend significant sums on hiring employees and training them in only to fail them when it comes to training up their managers.

Thankfully, decades of research on managerial prowess show us what good looks like when it comes to being an effective manager. Academics have identified a set of core traits and behaviours that distinguish effective managers from ineffective ones.

An effective manager is able to integrate certain personality traits (especially conscientiousness, extroversion and openness), interpersonal behaviours (communication, caring, trust building and ethical leadership) and decision-making competence with a people-oriented style.

Individuals like this outperform those who focus on a task-oriented approaches – hitting targets, getting through the to-do list – across most contexts studied.

This ties in with what workers say they value most at work. European workers put a safe environment for mental and physical health (71 per cent) and a trusting environment (69 per cent) ahead of good pay and benefits (66 per cent), according to Eurofound’s European Working Conditions Survey 2024.

A beginner’s guide to the 9-5 work week: Minimise your morning, don’t overshare

Are managers born or made? How many times have you heard “she’s a born leader” or “he really gets results”?

We assume that certain personality traits or behaviours automatically lead to promotion but research shows they might not be the things that make a manager truly effective. And that’s good news for introverts, more reflective personality types or those who’ve always thought, or felt, they’re not manager material.

An influential study in Personnel Psychology entitled Trait and Behavioural Theories of Leadership, led by Scott DeRue in 2011, was one of the first to explore which useful traits and effective behaviours worked best for managers. Over time, more studies have confirmed and built on their findings.

The most effective behaviours are a mix of transformational, task-oriented, relations-oriented, and change-oriented rather than a single universal style. Within those behaviours, problem-solving stands out as a particularly strong predictor of managerial effectiveness. The good news is that many of these behaviours can be taught and developed.

Managers who are perceived to be extroverts – or who fit stereotypical traits of what a leader looks or sounds like – have a definite advantage when it comes to getting the job but research shows that once they’re in the job, it’s behaviours such as agreeableness and emotional stability that help managers succeed in the role.

Unfortunately, organisations often promote people who put themselves forward or who excel at the technical aspects of the job, then just hope that their managerial skills miraculously emerge afterwards. Research suggests that such an approach can backfire, and that manager quality has a measurable effect on team results.

Selecting managers on their skills rather than desire to lead could substantially improve organisational performance, according to the findings.

Effective leadership appears to depend less on who looks or sounds like a leader than on the behaviours and skills they actually demonstrate. The most influential studies on effective managers have a clear answer: behaviours and skills matter more than demographics or personality traits.

If you’re a new manager, or even a seasoned one, here are some top tips based on research that shows which behaviours have the greatest positive impact.

  1. Make your expectations crystal clear: Agree specific, measurable goals with each individual so they know what success looks like from the start. Don’t make them waste time guessing what you need and want; just tell them.
  2. Give feedback little and often: Specific, timely comments and public recognition of positive contributions are among the most impactful behaviours for a manager. Team members need encouragement to feel motivated and it helps them know they’re progressing in the right direction.
  3. Listen actively, then act: People need to feel heard and valued. Working on your active listening skills – such as maintaining eye contact and not interrupting – build trust. Make sure you take notes of the conversation and follow through on what was agreed. Visible follow-through builds credibility and employee loyalty.
  4. Focus on the person, not just the role: Nobody wants to feel like they’re just a number, a key performance indicator (KPI) or a job description. Managers need to take time getting to know each team member and help them play to their strengths. Employees rank most highly managers who show care for them as individuals.
  5. Maintain an open-door policy: Managers’ availability and approachability are linked to higher levels of trust. Although you don’t have to physically keep your door ajar, you need to ensure staff know they can talk to you about most things at any time.
  6. Be fair: Integrity, fairness and humility predict trust and effectiveness.
  7. Manage yourself first: Self-awareness and emotional steadiness are what make managers effective, not just visible.
  8. Learn from peers: When you take on a role as a manager, lean on mentors and peers to help you increase learning quickly so these new skills stick.

This differs from “joint ownership”, where if one of the siblings were to die, their share would automatically pass to the other two – and so forth, to one owner.

“As these siblings are tenants in common, as and when each of them dies, their one-third share passes to their estate, not to the other surviving owners,” says Ferguson.

The will says the sister has the right to live in the property for life. But this wording is a bit redundant, says Ferguson. It is probably more of an expression of the parents’ wish for how things would go, she says.

“If you own a property as a tenant in common, you have an automatic right to live there for your period of ownership anyway,” says Ferguson. “So, any one of the three of them has the right to live there, actually.

“What the will doesn’t say is that the sister has an ‘exclusive right’ to live there. That would mean she had a ‘life interest’ which would postpone the legal ownership of her brothers,” says Ferguson.

“Because it doesn’t say ‘exclusive’, the other two have an equal right to live there if they want.”

This doesn’t mean that a nephew could just move into the property, for example.

“He is not an owner. I think that would need the consent of the other co-owners,” says Ferguson.

So, what happens to the house if the sister goes into residential care? The three siblings could agree to rent it out, with any profits split in three equal shares. Or the three could agree that a family member moves in as a caretaker.

Alternatively, if the three of them agree to it, the house could be sold.

There are some important things for the siblings to consider sooner rather than later.

“If one of them was to lose their mental capacity to make decisions, then you have a problem because you have a co-owner who cannot sign a contract or take a decision,” says Ferguson.

If there are concerns about the older sister, for example, and she still has mental capacity, talk to her about enduring power of attorney, Ferguson advises.

This is a legal document set up while you have full mental capacity to choose someone you trust, called your attorney, to manage your financial, property and/or personal affairs should you ever lose the capacity to do so yourself in the future.

“If she does that, then she has appointed someone in her place to sell the property, if they all decide that is the right thing to do,” says Ferguson.

If she did lose mental capacity and money was needed to pay for her residential care, for example, but an enduring power of attorney had not been arranged, her brothers would have to apply to court for a decision-making representative to be appointed for her.

Getting an enduring power of attorney in place now will be less time-consuming and expensive.

If the sister were to die before her brothers, her one-third share goes into her estate, to be administered in accordance with her will.

“If she has enough cash to pay the legacies she has made to the nieces, nephews, friends and charities mentioned in her will, then her share of the house would form part of the residue of her estate,” says Ferguson.

This residue is the part the sister says she wants to go to her brothers and sister-in-law. But money left as a legacy in a will takes priority over anything left in the residue – legacies get paid first.

So, if she didn’t have enough cash to pay the legacies, then eventually her one-third share of the house would have to be sold to fund the legacies, says Ferguson.

“The legacies have to be paid at some stage, and the executors won’t want to wait until everyone on the property title has died.

“The executors will look for agreement from the owners to sell the property to pay the legacies, or if the brothers wanted to keep the property, then they would have to fund those legacies.”

If the sister dies, will her sister-in-law, the reader, inherit her one-third share of the property?

Not exactly, says Ferguson.

“If the sister specifically left her share of the house to her sister-in-law, then that would take priority over the money legacies, but if she doesn’t, then whatever cash is there would first be used to pay the legacies and expenses,” says Ferguson.

If the reader’s husband dies, leaving everything to her in his will, then the reader will inherit his one-third share of the house. If he dies without a will, then two-thirds of his estate, including the house, would go to his wife and one-third to his children.

Ireland had the 11th highest weighted average rate in the euro area at the end of August, down from the ninth highest in July.

The weighted average interest rate on new fixed rate mortgage agreements, which constitute 94 per cent of the volume of new mortgage agreements, was 3.49 per cent in August, up one basis point from the previous month, the regulator said.

The figures also indicated the weighted average interest rate on household overnight deposits stood at 0.22 per cent in August.

Irish households are estimated to hold up to €175 billion on deposit with Irish banks, a substantial portion of held in overnight deposit accounts, which pay very low returns.

Retail banks here have been criticised for failing to increase their deposit rates in line with ECB levels while reporting big annual profits.

]]>yul38885 yul38885<![CDATA[Entry-level hiring in AI-augmented sectors drops by 16%]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/entry-level-hiring-in-ai-augmented-sectors-drops-by-16/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/entry-level-hiring-in-ai-augmented-sectors-drops-by-16/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 11:54:38 +0000Entry-level hiring in “AI-augmented occupations” in Ireland declined by 16 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, according to a new survey of labour market trends.

While IDA Ireland’s latest Labour Market Pulse report indicated that Ireland was entering the artificial intelligence (AI) era in “a position of strength”, ranking fourth globally for AI engineering talent, it warned there were “some emerging risks”.

Chief among them was the risk to graduate-level or junior recruitment.

It found that entry-level hiring in occupations that were using AI declined by 16.2 per cent (on an annual basis) between April and June this year, compared with a 10.8 per cent decline across those occupations overall.

“Within roles such as software engineering and data analysis, there are signs of a sharper pullback in junior recruitment, although the extent to which AI is driving this remains unclear,” it said.

The survey, produced in partnership with Microsoft and LinkedIn, was published to coincide with the International AI Summit taking place in Dublin this week, the flagship AI event of the State’s European Union presidency.

Oracle to cut another 70 jobs in Ireland in AI cost-cutting push

With more and more firms adopting AI, the survey found the State ranked fourth globally for AI engineering talent concentration, with 1.31 per cent of LinkedIn members in the Republic classified as AI engineering talent.

“Only Israel, Singapore and Luxembourg rank higher, with Ireland ahead of Germany, the UK and France,” the report noted.

The Republic also ranked fourth globally for net AI talent migration, indicating that the State continues to attract AI talent in an increasingly competitive global market.

While hiring here has moderated in line with international trends, the Irish labour market continues “to demonstrate greater resilience than selected European peers”, the report said.

In September, the LinkedIn hiring rate for the Republic was down 6.7 per cent year on year, compared with declines of 11.3 per cent in the UK and 18.1 per cent in Germany.

The report concluded the data showed “no clear evidence that the hiring slowdown is concentrated in jobs most exposed to AI or is disproportionately affecting entry-level recruitment”.

It noted that entry-level hiring declined by 8.3 per cent year on year in September, broadly in line with the 6.7 per cent decline in overall hiring.

“Ranking fourth in the world for AI talent sends a powerful signal to investors, and our focus now is on building on that advantage through continued investment in talent, infrastructure and adoption,” said IDA Ireland chief executive Michael Lohan.

Minister for Enterprise Peter Burke said: “The Irish labour market is performing well with employment levels and rates remaining high, and unemployment low at close to 5 per cent. Ireland has moved quickly in adopting AI, with strong AI usage and diffusion across our economy.

“We need to stay ahead and build on this momentum to fully reap the benefits from AI, a core theme of this week’s International AI Summit as part of Ireland’s EU presidency.”

The Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance (UINR) has reported the discovery of 30 human remains at a site in Poland where Polish partisans killed Ukrainian civilians during World War Two.

The head of the UINR, Oleksandr Alfyorov, thanked Poland for granting permission to conduct research at the location, which he said would help advance “true reconciliation” between the two countries over their difficult shared history.

Ukraine has likewise recently allowed Poland to search for and exhume the remains of Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists during the war.

At the end of August, the Polish authorities approved a request from Ukraine to conduct a search in the village of Łasków in southeastern Poland, around 10km from the border with Ukraine.

On 10 March 1944, units of the Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasant Battalions (Bataliony Chłopskie), two major Polish underground resistance movements that emerged during the Nazi-German occupation, attacked Łasków, which had a predominantly ethnic Ukrainian population.

Estimates suggest that around 300 civilians were killed. Among them was a local Orthodox priest, Lev Korobchuk.

On the same day, members of the Home Army also attacked the nearby village of Sahryń, where they are estimated to have killed hundreds more Ukrainians. Ukraine has also submitted an application to carry out exploratory work there.

Poland has granted permission for Ukraine to conduct a search for the remains of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish resistance fighters during WWII https://t.co/4JeAAhYJcY

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 2, 2026

Work began in Łasków on 6 October and, on Wednesday this week, the UINR announced that it had “discovered the remains of 30 victims…[who] died as a result of the attack of the units of the Home Army and the Peasant Battalion in March 1944″.

Svyatoslav Sheremeta, the head of the Lviv-based Dolya memorial and search centre, which carried out the work on behalf of the UINR, said that they now hope to “conduct exhumation, rebury the dead, and honour their memory with dignity”.

“Thank you to the Polish side for the opportunity to conduct research,” added Alfyorov. “Our common task is to ensure a worthy commemoration of all victims, regardless of their origin and nationality.”

“True reconciliation begins with respect for everyone’s memory, recognition of the pain of the other side, and the common desire for understanding,” said the head of UNIP, which shared images from the search site in Łasków’s Orthodox cemetery.

 

At the time of writing, Polish officials had not yet commented on the development. However, when search work began last week, Rafał Kościański, a spokesman for Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), told Radio Lublin that IPN staff were participating as observers.

Wiesław Koman, from the Provincial Office for the Protection of Monuments, added that cooperation between Polish and Ukrainian archaeologists at the site had been “impeccable”.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ambassador to Poland, Vasyl Bodnar, told the broadcaster that the work in Łasków was “a step towards reconciliation between our nations”.

“This is happening on both sides of the border and demonstrates the openness of both sides to commemorating the victims of the past conflict,” said Bodnar. “There are differing voices from different sides of the political arena, but this is the right path, one we should have been on for a long time.”

Polish and Ukrainian researchers have exhumed the remains of 115 Polish soldiers who died in 1939 defending Lviv – now in Ukraine but then part of Poland and known as Lwów – during the invasions by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union at the start of WWII https://t.co/yQNeq2D54E

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 2, 2026

The legacy of wartime massacres has long overshadowed relations between Poland and Ukraine, who have otherwise become close allies since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

In 2017, Ukraine imposed a ban on searches on its territory for Polish victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists massacred around 100,000 ethnic Poles, mostly women and children.

Poland has recognised those massacres as a genocide. Ukraine rejects the use of that term, and also points to anti-Ukrainian repression in the interwar Polish state and the massacres of Ukrainian civilians carried out by Polish partisans during the war.

In a diplomatic breakthrough last year, Kyiv agreed to lift its moratorium on exhumations. Since then, it has granted permission for Poland to conduct searches and exhumations at a number of locations.

The remains of 55 Poles massacred by Ukrainian nationalists in WWII have been reburied at a ceremony in Ukraine attended by political and religious figures from both countries.

The victims, around half of them children, were exhumed this summer https://t.co/4q3giZhBAL

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2026

However, tensions over historical issues reemerged this year, when President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”, the group that led the Volhynia massacres.

That prompted his Polish counterpart, Karol Nawrocki, to strip Zelensky of Poland’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle.

However, the two sides subsequently made efforts to reach a diplomatic solution, including a pledge by Zelensky to “grant a substantial number of permits for search and exhumation work”

Poland’s energy ministry has signed an agreement with two state-owned companies, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) and Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE), setting out responsibilities for preparing for the construction of Poland’s planned second nuclear power plant.

“This is an investment in our security, sovereignty and economic development,” declared energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Having our own stable energy sources strengthens Poland’s resilience to crises and reduces dependence on external suppliers.”

❗️ @ME_GOV_PL, @PEJ_PL i @Grupa_PGE podpisały dziś porozumienie określające zasady współpracy przy przygotowaniu budowy drugiej polskiej elektrowni jądrowej 🇵🇱

Polska jest 20. gospodarką świata, ale nasze ambicje sięgają wyżej. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh

— Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026

Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project.

PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant.

However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis.

 

The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year.

Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation.

According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule.

The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026

Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts.

The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables.

Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).

]]> Everything you need to know one year ahead of Poland’s parliamentary elections https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/15/everything-you-need-to-know-one-year-ahead-of-polands-parliamentary-elections/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 09:48:11 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105449 Daniel Tilles Polling suggests the outcome is too close to call.]]>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it has the support of a majority in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. If that does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president.

Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions.

Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Poland has in recent years also moved to strengthen its ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. This year, Polish and Norwegian companies announced plans to develop a new anti-drone system for Poland in the wake of incursions of Russian drones into Polish airspace.

Last year, Norway opened a facility in Poland, Camp Jomsborg, for training Ukrainian military personnel. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.

The two countries also have close energy ties. In 2022, the Baltic Pipe began delivering Norwegian gas to Poland, helping the country reduce its reliance on Russian supplies. Norway’s Equinor is also involved in developing one of Poland’s first offshore wind farms in the Baltic.

Poland will manufacture the missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is buying from South Korea.

The Norwegian government says that Polish production "will strengthen security of supply for Norway and other European customers of the system" https://t.co/NIJj7owK45

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 29, 2026

Poland has also moved closer in recent years to Sweden, with which it signed a strategic partnership in 2024. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.

Last year, at Poland’s suggestion, NATO launched a new military mission to protect critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea.

On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia.

On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”.

He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”.

Na zlecenie polskich służb niemiecka policja zatrzymała dwóch obywateli tureckich podejrzanych o podpalenie stacji Starlink na Mazowszu. To kolejny akt wojny hybrydowej. Sprawcy sabotażu odpowiedzą przed polskim wymiarem sprawiedliwości.

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Shortly afterwards, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński revealed that the arrests had taken place in cooperation between Poland’s police and Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA).

He said that the charge the suspects are likely to face in Poland would be “sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service”, a crime that carries a minimum prison sentence of 10 years, ranging up to life.

Later on Monday, Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister in charge of the security services, confirmed that Poland believes the attack was carried out “on behalf of the Russian security services”.

 

The incident in question took place on 23 September at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which has relied heavily on Starlink connections since Russia’s full-scale invasion.

Firefighters were called out that evening to a fire at the facility, which is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel. The next day, digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gakowski revealed that the blaze had been started deliberately and “the modus operandi is clearly Russian”.

Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. Those have included a series of arson attacks, including one that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre and another at a drone factory that is used to supply the Ukrainian military.

A fire last night at a Starlink ground station in Poland that is used to provide internet services to Ukraine was caused deliberately and "the modus operandi is clearly Russian", says digital affairs minister @KGawkowski https://t.co/p2DEn7XexF

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026

On Monday evening, at a press conference alongside Kierwiński and Siemoniak, the commander of Poland’s police, Marek Boroń, revealed that one of the two Turkish suspects had resident status in Germany while the other did not.

He said that the Polish authorities had been able to document their movements in Poland, and had recordings, fingerprints and DNA of the suspects.

Simoniak added that there was a “high probability” that other individuals were involved in the attack, but that he could not divulge further information about them currently. He also thanked the German authorities for their cooperation.

“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said the minister, quoted by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. “And it’s worth adding that Russian intelligence services are increasingly using people connected to the criminal world. They never use their own citizens.”

Russia uses individuals already present in Europe – and often already involved in criminal activity – to carry out most of its hybrid operations. On Monday, in a separate case, three Ukrainians and one Belarusian went on trial in Warsaw accused of being behind a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania.

Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026

On Tuesday morning, German newspaper Handelsblatt reported confirmation from the State Criminal Police Office (LKA) in Baden-Württemberg that two Turkish men had been detained on Monday in the town of Nürtingen at the request of the Polish authorities.

The office did not provide further details, but Handelsblatt reports that the two suspects are due to be brought before a judge today.

Four men have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders.

The accused – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – can be named only as Oleksandr H., Stepan K., Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. under Polish privacy law and their trial is taking place behind closed doors for security reasons.

Polish prosecutors say that they were part of an organised group tasked with “committing acts of sabotage and terrorism” on behalf of Russia’s foreign intelligence service in April and May 2024.

Those included a fire that burned down Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, Marywilska 44; another at a store in Warsaw belonging to home improvement chain OBI; and a third at an IKEA store in Vilnius. They also allegedly planned an arson attack on an IKEA store in the Latvian capital of Riga.

W Sądzie Okręgowym Warszawa-Praga ruszył proces grupy przestępczej, która miała na zlecenie Federacji Rosyjskiej podpalać markety wielkopowierzchniowe, w tym centrum handlowe przy Marywilskiej w Warszawie.https://t.co/0CFl1RyJvq

— TVN Warszawa (@tvnwarszawa) October 12, 2026

According to an indictment issued against the men in March this year, Stepan K., the Belarusian, set fire to the OBI store. Oleksandr H. is accused of involvement in the arson attack on the IKEA store in Vilnius and preparations for further attacks.

The pair have been indicted under Poland’s espionage law for carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism on behalf of foreign intelligence. That crime carries a minimum sentence of 10 years in prison, ranging up to life.

Another Ukrainian suspect, Daniil B., had also been due to stand trial today on the same charge, with prosecutors finding that he had received an order from a handler in Russia to go to Marywilska on the night the arson attack took place and record footage of the fire and the response of the emergency services.

However, Daniil B. was jailed in Lithuania last year for his role in the Vilnius IKEA fire and Poland has not yet managed to secure his extradition for the trial in Warsaw, meaning that it went ahead without his involvement.

Polish prosecutors say they have determined that the Marywilska fire was also carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence, but have not been able to identify which individuals actually perpetrated the attack.

 

Stepan K. and Oleksandr H. – as well as Vitalii K., whom prosecutors accuse of helping carry out the arson in Vilnius – are additionally charged with participating in an organised criminal group that aimed to carry out terrorist offences, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison.

Both Vitalii K. and Pavlo T. were also indicted in relation to an assault in the village of Wólka Kosowska, just outside Warsaw.

Pavlo T. was already convicted in Poland last year along with two other Ukrainian men, Serhii R. and Vladyslav Y., over their role in the same criminal group tasked with carrying out acts of sabotage and terrorism by Russia. They were handed jail terms ranging from 16 months to five and a half years.

Two other alleged members of the group, Serhii Chalyi and Oleksandr Varyvoda, who prosecutors say were involved in coordinating sabotage activities, remain wanted.

Three Ukrainians have been jailed in Poland for their role in a group tasked with carrying out sabotage and terrorism.

That included the fire that destroyed Warsaw’s largest shopping centre, which Polish prosecutors say was carried out on Russia’s orders https://t.co/xuFx5T4HH9

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2025

In response to evidence that Moscow was behind the Marywilska fire, Poland last year ordered Russia’s consulate in Kraków to close. It has since closed all Russian consulates due to Moscow’s ongoing campaign of sabotage, with Russia responding by shutting down all Polish consulates on its territory.

A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russian sabotage in Europe.

Most recently, Poland has accused Moscow of being behind a fire at a drone factory that supplies the Polish and Ukrainian militaries. Last year, Ukrainian operatives working on behalf of Russia also used explosives in an attempt to derail a train in Poland.

Most acts of sabotage ordered by Russia in Poland have been carried out not by Russians themselves, but by Ukrainians and Belarusians, large numbers of whom already live in Poland and other countries in the region.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

Czy to możliwe, że państwo traci kontrolę nad własnym systemem inwigilacji? I to nie była stara konsola…

Z opinii biegłych ABW wynika, że CBA kupiło narzędzie, nad którym nie miało pełnej kontroli. Dane opuszczały Polskę, moduł infekujący kontrolował producent, a zagraniczna…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 12, 2026

The ABW experts also highlighted serious concerns over management and security of the harvested data, noting that Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (CBA), which was responsible for using the spyware, “did not have full control over the Pegasus system”.

“The CBA did not have passwords to access some accounts with administrative privileges and some system components remained under the control of the manufacturer [NSO],” wrote the prosecutor’s office. “The server module responsible for infecting mobile devices remained under the manufacturer’s exclusive control.”

Data transmitted through the Pegasus system travelled outside Polish territory, through “servers located in various parts of the world”, in a network managed by NSO and “beyond the CBA’s control”, found the experts.

Meanwhile, NSO “had technical access to materials from operational surveillance”, although prosecutors say that the experts “did not determine whether the manufacturer actually obtained access to materials from specific operations”.

The former deputy head of Poland’s Central Anti-Corruption Bureau has been charged with unlawfully sharing material obtained through surveillance using Pegasus spyware, including communication involving PM @donaldtusk's daughter when Tusk was in opposition https://t.co/LyTuqbq0KQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2025

In a video commenting on the latest findings, Tusk said that the investigation into Pegasus was “coming to a head”. He called it “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history after the fall of communism”.

The former PIS authorities signed a contract for a spyware system “over which they de facto had no control, because control remained in the hands of Israel and an Israeli company…whose cooperation with Israeli intelligence is, of course, beyond doubt”, said the prime minister.

“They paid money for a system that de facto transferred all possible data on Polish citizens, Polish opposition leaders and Polish independent prosecutors…to the Israeli side,” he added. “This is no longer [just] a scandal…We’re talking about a crime against the state.”

Two former heads of Polish security agencies have been charged over the use of Pegasus spyware under the former PiS government.

The pair, who deny wrongdoing, could be jailed for up to three years if found guilty of unlawfully allowing use of the spyware https://t.co/TWjQR74IYT

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 26, 2026

Later on Monday, a separate parliamentary committee set up by the ruling coalition to investigate the use of Pegasus also revealed unclassified sections of a report on its findings.

In addition to the information released by prosecutors, the commission also said that the CBA had never obtained the required IT security accreditation for Pegasus, meaning that it was used without meeting requirements for protecting classified information.

The commission’s chairwoman, Magdalena Sroka, also said that courts granting authorisation for the use of Pegasus were not informed of its full capabilities, such as the ability to access the entire contents of phones, reports broadcaster RMF.

💬 Jest to dokument o tym, jak władza publiczna w Polsce sięgnęła po narzędzie ingerujące w prawa obywatelskie – powiedziała przewodnicząca komisji śledczej ds. inwigilacji systemem Pegasus @MagdalenaSroka, prezentując raport z prac komisji.https://t.co/MzA9gj4M0Y

— PolsatNews.pl (@PolsatNewsPL) October 12, 2026

Legal proceedings are already underway against a number of former officials in relation to Pegasus. In February, prosecutors charged the former heads of the AWB and Military Counterintelligence Service (SKW) with abuse of power for approving the use of Pegasus despite being aware of legal shortcomings.

Previously, the former head of the CBA was charged with the same offence, while one of his deputies was charged with unlawfully disclosing material from surveillance of Roman Giertych, an MP from Tusk’s KO party who has also worked as a lawyer for Tusk and his family.

Last year, a former deputy justice minister from the PiS government, Michał Woś, was indicted to stand trial over his role in the alleged illegal use of justice ministry funds to help the CBA purchase Pegasus.

The United States wants Poland to join the G20 “as soon as possible” and intends to raise the issue with other members of the international forum at its forthcoming summit in December in Miami, the US State Department has told the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Having previously endorsed Polish membership of the G20 in May, the US now says it intends to “continue discussions with G20 members this year on making Poland a full member as soon as possible”.

“Poland’s long-term and steady economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant,” the State Department told PAP.

Stany Zjednoczone oficjalnie zadeklarowały, że będą zabiegać o stałe członkostwo Polski w G20 https://t.co/lnZ583HIus

— Fakty RMF FM (@RMF24pl) October 11, 2026

The G20, a major intergovernmental forum that brings together 19 major countries together with the European Union and the African Union, is set to meet at a golf resort owned by President Donald Trump in Miami on 14-15 December. Poland is also participating this year as a guest of the United States.

PAP reports that the US has proposed that one of the points in the final declaration adopted by leaders at the conclusion of the summit refer to Poland’s permanent membership. However, this would require the assent of all current members, including Russia.

The issue is likely to be discussed in a pre-summit online meeting of so-called “sherpas” negotiating the text of the declaration, reports PAP.

 

After visiting Washington earlier this month, Marcin Przydacz, the head of President Karol Nawrocki’s international policy office, said that joining the G20 permanently is “Plan A”, but acknowledged that receiving a consensus from existing member states made this variant difficult.

He added that Nawrocki would travel to London before the summit to discuss the possibility of continuing Poland’s guest status next year, when the UK will host the G20. At a meeting of G20 trade ministers last week, finance minister Andrzej Domański said that Poland has a good chance of being invited next year.

Nawrocki also plans to visit G20 members Saudi Arabia and Argentina to canvass for support for Poland’s membership bid, Przydacz has confirmed.

A third option would be for Poland to become a “permanent guest”, a status typically reserved for organisations like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group, but also held by Spain.

The United States has expressed "strong support for Poland’s accession to the G20 as a permanent member" following talks in Warsaw, after which it also emphasised "strong and growing" Polish-American relations https://t.co/qTpCACnMfu

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 2, 2026

Poland has long lobbied for membership in the group. In 2010, then-President Lech Kaczyński said “the place of my country is among the members of the G20”. In 2022, following the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Polish government argued that their country should replace Russia.

Last December, the US invited Poland to join this year’s summit. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Poland was “assuming its rightful place” at the forum.

Poland has argued that its membership is justified by its economy being on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world.

Though G20 membership is not decided solely on that basis, the G20 does include most of the world’s 20 largest economies (only Switzerland and the Netherlands have larger economies than Poland but no G20 membership).

Polish President @NawrockiKn “does not like” the fact that Donald Trump has invited Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami, says his chief foreign policy aide.

However, Nawrocki still plans to attend the event, which Poland is invited to as a guest https://t.co/JojsFB4NX6

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 26, 2026

In September, the United States provoked criticism from European leaders, including Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski, when it announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin would be invited to the Miami summit.

Subsequently, Przydacz confirmed that, although Nawrocki, who is a close ally of Trump, “does not like” the fact that Putin has been invited, the Polish president was still planning to attend the summit.

Sikorski likewise said he would attend a G20 meeting of foreign ministers in Atlanta in October even if a Russian representative was there and agreed that Poland should not boycott the summit in December.
