Shares in Britain’s banking giants tumbled this morning after new reports suggested John Healey is set to raise taxes on lenders when he delivers his first Budget at the end of the month.

Natwest dropped two per cent to 660.40p, while Lloyds was down around 2.5 per cent to 103.40p. Barclays slid 0.4 per cent to 430.50p as markets opened

The Chancellor has faced fierce lobbying from the left of the Labour party and trade unions to slap higher taxes on the sector following the bumper profits reaped by industry this year.

Healey is now understood to have decided to target the sector for a cash raid as he looks to balance the books on 28 October, The Guardian has reported.

The simplest lever available to Healey would be an increase to the banking surcharge that sits on top of corporation tax. The surcharge currently sits at three per cent after being reduced from eight per cent under Jeremy Hunt’s Chancellorship in 2023.

A reversal of that move is understood to be under discussion, which would raise around £2bn a year.

But some have urged the Chancellor to go even further with a windfall tax on the profits of lenders. Activists at Positive Money say such a move could raise £19bn from the coffers of Natwest, Lloyds, Barclays and HSBC alone.

Speaking to reporters in Bangkok for the IMF summit, Healey said: “My observation on the banks is that people too often see ​them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future ⁠prospects.”

He added there was “decisions to take in the budget”.

In a separate interview with Bloomberg Television, Healey described banks as “a part of the jewel … in the British economic crown”.

Healey set for bank tax row with City

Any announcement is set to spark uproar in the City, whose efforts to shield the sector from a tax raid appear to have gone unheeded. Industry bosses have raised concerns that banks already face an outsized tax rate when compared with competitors overseas. Figures from PwC show total taxes on UK banks amount to 46 per cent of profits, compared to 42 percent in Amsterdam, 39 per cent in Frankfurt, 29 per cent in Dublin and 28 per cent in Dublin.

A cohort of City bosses – including the chiefs of TheCityUK, CBI and UK Finance – warned Healey in a letter last week that “a higher tax burden may not necessarily generate higher tax receipts if capital, people and businesses move elsewhere”.

Tory leader Kemi Badenoch joined the defensive ranks against a bank tax earlier this week after firing a warning shot to Healey during a visit to Edinburgh.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “Britain needs growth. But a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it. Labour should be backing businesses and wealth-creators, not making their lives even harder.”

The top bosses of HSBC, Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and Santander were called in for a meeting with Healey last week, where the Chancellor remained tight-lipped on fiscal policy but warned of the “challenging” fiscal landscape.

Economists have forecast Healey’s £24bn in headroom has more than halved following the surge in borrowing costs tied to the inflationary impact of the US-Iran war.

A Treasury spokesperson said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

    New inheritance tax rules will drastically alter how people use their pensions, and put a lot of individuals in difficult positions, writes Steve Gauke

    For years, pensions have been one of the most effective ways for families to pass wealth to the next generation. But from April 2027, that will change, with most unused pension funds being brought into the scope of inheritance tax.

    The problem isn’t simply that more families will face an inheritance tax bill. It’s that many may not realise they’re affected until it’s too late to prepare. We risk sleepwalking into a situation where thousands of families face unexpected tax liabilities at an already difficult time. Many families have planned around the old legislation, leaving a potential knowledge gap between the government distributing the new rules and the families who must understand them.

    The scale of the change is significant; the government’s estimates suggest that around 10,500 estates will pay inheritance tax for the first time in 2027 to 2028, and that a further 38,500 will pay more, with the average bill expected to rise by around £34,000. These are, of course, only estimates, but the changes will drastically alter how people use their pensions in response. This shift will put a lot of individuals in difficult positions, after all, behind every one of those figures is a family who will be asked to find a large sum of money at a very difficult time. When you consider the cost of living crisis, and how many families are asset rich but cash poor, changes like these will have a huge impact on people’s lives.

    The pension changes coming into effect in April 2027 may increase the inheritance tax payable by affected estates, potentially leaving beneficiaries with a larger tax bill and a smaller inheritance than anticipated. This adds to existing cash-flow pressures: beneficiaries can wait six to 12 months for their inheritance, while inheritance tax is generally due by the end of the sixth month after death. The changes won’t necessarily lengthen that wait, but executors usually need to pay the tax, or the first instalment where instalments are permitted, before obtaining probate. Under the new rules, beneficiaries may only be able to access around half of the affected pension benefits for up to 15 months. 

    This is the core of the problem. On paper families are inheriting a significant amount of wealth. But in practice, they have very little cash available to pay the bills in front of them. The good news is that families still have time to prepare. The first step is to have open conversations about inheritance; however uncomfortable they may feel. Understand what an estate is likely to include, locate important documents and establish whether the upcoming changes could create an inheritance tax liability.

    It’s also important to consider how any tax bill would actually be paid. Seeking independent financial advice, understanding the available payment arrangements and exploring options for accessing funds where necessary can help prevent difficult decisions being made under pressure. For example, a probate or inheritance loan, gives families early access to part of their inheritance, so that nobody is forced into a hurried sale.

    Families will plan around whatever the rules are, but what they need now from the government is clarity, enough time to prepare and some flexibility when the system moves more slowly than the bills arrive. Inheritance should not become an unnecessary financial burden simply because families were unaware of the rules or unable to access their money when they needed it most.

    Steve Gauke is managing director at Provira

    NIMBYs and rising migration have both been blamed for the UK's housing shortage. What's the actual problem, asks Ben Hopkinson.]]>

    NIMBYs and rising migration have both been blamed for the UK’s housing shortage. What’s the actual problem, asks Ben Hopkinson

    It is clear that the UK does not have enough homes for its population. There are two stories about why this has happened. The first, told by YIMBYs, is that it is simply too hard to build homes and expand the housing supply. The other, told by migration hawks, is that the record numbers entering Britain have driven up demand for scarce properties. Both have a truth to them, and action solely on one is not enough to end the housing crisis. 

    How bad is the UK’s housing shortage?

    Of all the major Western European countries, the UK has the second fewest homes per 1,000 people. To catch up to the average, the UK needs 6.9m more homes. This number has grown from 6.5m homes using 2023 data, as net migration has outpaced our ability to build homes, which isn’t true for most other European countries. England accounts for 6.2m of those missing homes.

    Historically, the UK, and especially England, has not built enough homes. Since the early 1980s, France has grown its housing stock by an average of 1.07 per cent a year, while England has only managed 0.82 per cent a year. This may seem like a small difference, but it adds up after four decades of compounding.

    England has averaged only 178,000 homes a year. Matching France’s housing stock growth would require building 246,000 homes a year. Achieving the government’s 300,000 home a year target would be useful for helping to close the gap. Sadly it is almost certain to be missed, with even Angela Rayner, the re-appointed housing secretary, conceding the manifesto commitment was actually a ‘stretch target’.

    Had England matched France’s building rate since the early 1980s, it would have 2.9m additional homes. This alone would have been enough to close half of England’s housing shortage. 

    Every single year, France has expanded its housing stock faster than its population has grown. England cannot say the same. After barely rising from the mid-2000s, England’s homes per 1,000 peaked in 2021. Since then, high levels of migration have reduced this number. This means that the housing shortage is getting worse despite 1.1m homes being built since 2020.

    This is where the migration hawk story comes in, with claims that large-scale migration has driven up demand for our paltry supply of homes. 

    Has migration contributed?

    Had net migration been capped at 100,000 a year since 1997, and the rate of housebuilding remained unchanged, England would now have 473 homes per 1,000. That makes up about a third of the gap that England has with the rest of Western Europe.

    The recent spike of migration has given further credence to the demand-side story. Had net migration stayed in the tens of thousands since 2020 instead of the record-breaking wave, house prices would be roughly £15,270, or 5.2 per cent, lower in England. This spike in migration could be the missing puzzle piece that explains why high interest rates have not had the catastrophic impact on house prices that many predicted.

    So where do these two stories leave us? Building an achievable number of homes could have closed half the gap, while keeping to the oft-made manifesto pledge of tens of thousands not hundreds of thousands of net migrants would have closed a third of the gap. Both help explain why there are so few homes per capita in the UK. Combined, they would have come close to ending the housing shortage. 

    The mismatch between high demand and low supply drives many of the symptoms of the housing crisis: the unaffordability of properties, smaller and lower quality homes, and the young being priced out of home ownership. 

    We don’t have a time machine to change the policy decisions made decades ago that have caused the housing crisis. But the policy choices taken today and after the next general election will decide whether we make progress in closing our housing shortage or allow it to grow even more. 

    Ben Hopkinson is the head of housing and infrastructure at the Centre for Policy Studies

    Tens of thousands of taxpayers were handed money back from HMRC last year after savers had too much tax deducted from their pension withdrawals, City AM can reveal.

    HMRC processed 54,166 pension withdrawal repayments in the 2025/26 financial year, worth around £188m, according to figures obtained through a Freedom of Information request.

    During the financial year, HMRC received 107,880 repayment claim forms. On average, impacted savers were repaid roughly £3,470.

    The overtaxation by the department stemmed from default Pay As You Earn (PAYE) rules used to collect income tax. The PAYE system is the government’s primary method for collecting income tax, national insurance and student loan payments directly from an employee’s wage slip.

    It also deducts taxes from private or workplace pension withdrawals. Under current rules Brits can access their pension pot from age 55, with 25 per cent of the total value of the pot taken tax-free.

    But in some circumstances, a single withdrawal can be treated as monthly income, as pension providers rarely hold an up-to-date tax code for customers, leading HMRC to tax the withdrawal as though it were regular income.

    Savers must apply for money back instead of HMRC issuing an automatic refund.

    Steve Webb, partner at pensions consultant LCP and former pensions minister, described the need to file a form to recover the money as “absurd” and an unnecessary burden for the department and taxpayers.

    “The whole system of overtaxing people on pension withdrawals and expecting them to fill in one of three different claim forms to get their tax back is absurd…. a huge waste of taxpayer time and effort,” he said.

    “For most people, the right answer will turn out to be that they need to have basic rate tax deducted at source and that should be what happens. For people who turn out to have been higher rate taxpayers at the end of the year it is a simple matter to collect the rest through the end year assessment process. This system is run purely for the convenience of HMRC rather than the taxpayer and is long overdue for reform.”

    ‘Waste of taxpayer time’

    The vast majority of refunded money was claimed through P55 forms, which covers partial withdrawals, with £124.5m returned across 37,116 claims.

    Brits who filled in P53Z forms, used by people who have completely wiped out their retirement pot but can still rely on other income, had £51.8m paid out from 14,372 claims. Meanwhile, an additional £10.8m was refunded across 2,519 P50Z form claims, which covers those who have no other existing income. 

    Nearly 160 claimants also used niche defined benefit forms in a bid to get money back, including P55DB, P53ZDB and P502DB. In total, savers who filed for a refund using these forms received around £0.85m.

    HMRC noted that it works through every case and does not reject claims, but not all applicants receive a payout, with only roughly half of the claims resulting in repayment.

    HMRC said: “This depends entirely on their personal circumstances…whether this is an underpayment for a previous year, if they have ongoing employment, and whether the pension has been taxed at the correct rate of tax.”

    Increasing awareness

    HMRC’s failure to immediately contact savers who were overtaxed means only those who spot the error and file a claim can attempt to get back their cash immediately.

    Others who do not identify the overcharge or choose not to submit a claim, typically have to wait until HMRC runs its end of financial year tax reconciliation process, meaning many often wait months for funds.

    HMRC said it could not provide the total number of people whose pension withdrawals had been overtaxed, or the total amount of tax over-deducted, without reviewing individual customer records.

    The findings come amid both HMRC and the Department of Work and Pensions (DWP) urging people to become more engaged with their pensions to prevent being overcharged and missing out on other financial benefits.

    According to statistics released by the DWP in May, the proportion of overpaid Pension Credit claims increased to 33 per cent in the 2025/26 tax year, up from 28 per cent the prior year.

    The two drivers behind incorrect payments were identified as claimants failing to fully declare their financial assets or spending time overseas that surpassed the limit that benefit rules permit. By April 2031, the government expects to save £370m.

    But despite the crackdown on Pension Credit claims, the benefit remains widely unclaimed by those who qualify for the payment.

    The head of the International Monetary Fund has warned financial ministers that widespread AI adoption could erode tax bases across the world as incomes are squeezed by the technology.

    Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the IMF, said governments may be ill-prepared for a potential slump in tax revenue brought on by AI’s impact on the labour market. 

    At the fund’s summit in Bangkok, Georgieva has issued a series of warnings on the impact of AI, calling the technology a “slow-moving tsunami” that could affect 60 per cent of jobs in wealthy countries. 

    In a blog post on Thursday, Georgieva suggested governments would need to “make hard choices” and implement vast tax reform to shift revenue streams from labour to other areas such as land or investment. 

    “AI may raise growth, but it could also reduce labour income, increase inequality, and erode the tax base,” Georgieva said. “Countries will need fiscal space to invest in infrastructure and skills, and cushion the impact on the most vulnerable. And they will need tax systems designed for the AI era. 

    “With debt already high, policymakers will need to make hard choices.”

    AI’s toll on the tax system

    In the UK, income taxes account for more than a quarter of total tax receipts. National Insurance paid by workers and employers is another large revenue-raiser, accounting for about 16 per cent of total receipts in 2025-26. 

    Revenue is also largely made from levies on the highest earners as the top one per cent pay about 28.5 per cent of all tax. 

    Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the launch of the UK’s AI Economics Institute, which is being led by Nobel prize winner Professor Simon Johnson, in order to evaluate and manage the effects that the technology could have on fiscal policy. 

    Oxford professor Ben Ansell weighed in on the debate by proposing an “AI token tax”, which would be a levy on the use of models. The Austrian-American economist Anton Korinek, who sits on Anthropic’s economic advisory council, has said that governments should transition from income taxation to consumption taxation. 

    In her warning on AI, Georgieva also said that there could be a fall in stock prices that “cascades through the highly leveraged and circular AI ecosystem”, with losses “spread around the world”. 

    Her statements echo those of Financial Stability Board chair Andrew Bailey and Bank of England deputy governor Sarah Breeden, who predicted there would be a “correction” in market pricing if company profits disappoint following years of heavy capital investment in AI.

    Risks to AI firms and governments come at a tumultuous time for the global economy given ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East and low growth in Western economies. 

    The IMF urged European countries to avoid imposing more protectionist measures, after its ‘Made in Europe’ scheme – designed to boost domestic manufacturers over imports from China – has come under the spotlight. 

    Economists advised European leaders to dismiss “rising calls for more interventionist industrial policy” as they would not “durably address Europe’s underlying growth problem”. 

    Given large deficits in various major economies across the continent, ministers were also urged to only provide energy support packages that were “tightly targeted at supporting the most vulnerable”.

    Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt says the Fifa Council is still being denied full transparency over Gianni Infantino’s aborted World Cup sell-off plan.

    Infantino apologised to the Council today as it met for the first time since controversy erupted over Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), a new private company Infantino lined up investors for without telling the governing body’s supposed steering committee.

    But Hewitt said she hadn’t changed her view that Infantino may be criminally culpable, in the absence of documentation she insisted she had repeatedly asked for.

    “We didn’t get answers to anything that we had specifically requested, for example getting the papers from FFE,” she said.

    “I asked the question ‘why not?’ – and we were asked to submit those questions in writing.

    “I think the man has to answer those questions and if he doesn’t answer those questions now, he’s not fit to be Fifa president – and that was what was shared in the meeting.

    “I’ve repeatedly asked for the papers to be shared. I haven’t received them and still, in spite of the request today, I haven’t received them.”

    Hewitt said she wanted transparency over Infantino’s role in FFE, the Folarin Balogun red card furore at this summer’s World Cup and the awarding of the Fifa Peace Prize to Donald Trump.

    “That will be the point at which we can say that any individual that was involved in FFE can or cannot be trusted. Because until we see what actually happened it’s very difficult to say behaviour needs or not to change.”

    A group of Lloyd’s syndicates have sought to block £45m in defence funding for two former Petrofac executives facing a criminal bribery trial.

    The group of syndicates provided directors’ and officers’ (D&O) insurance coverage to Petrofac’s former chief operating officer, Marwan Chedid, and former chief operations officer George Salibi.

    Chedid and Salibi rely on Petrofac’s D&O insurance to cover their legal costs, but the insurers argued the alleged fraud violated the policy. The Lloyd’s underwriters filed a claim in the High Court in August to withdraw the coverage.

    In September, Mr Justice Jacobs ruled that the insurers cannot withhold funding and must continue to cover them unless the bribery allegations are proven in court. The parties were at the Court of Appeal on Thursday as several syndicates sought to overturn the ruling.

    The costs were covered under a primary and first excess policy, whose limits were nearly exhausted, but the reinsurers provided a second layer of coverage with a £45m limit.

    Of the nine insurance firms listed to appeal, only four appealed the ruling, with two being Lloyd’s syndicates Samford Underwriting and Gracechurch UTG (formerly known as ANV). Resinsurance firms MS Amlin and MSI are also appealing. One of the claimants, Liberty Managing Agency, confirmed to City AM that it was not appealing.

    SFO trial to commence in November

    The Serious Fraud Office (SFO) brought criminal charges against Chedid and Salibi in February 2024 for allegedly offering and paying agents over $30m to influence the awarding of contracts worth about $3.3bn in Petrofac’s favour.

    The alleged contracts relate to oil facilities in the UAE, including one for the infrastructure and design of the Gulf’s second-largest oil field, the Upper Zakum Field Development Project.

    Both Chedid and Salibi both have pleaded not guilty to the charges. The SFO confirmed to City AM that the trial against Chedid and Salibi, which was due to start on 2 November, will begin on 23 November at Southwark Crown Court.

    Petrofac pleaded guilty on 4 October 2021 to seven counts of failing to prevent bribery under the UK Bribery Act.

    “This is a very important case for the insurance industry, for white-collar criminal defendants and defence practitioners,” Macfarlanes partner, Lorna Emson, told City AM.

    Peppa Pig and the Lionesses isn’t the most obvious pairing. One’s a muddy-puddle-loving pig loved by my kids and toddlers everywhere and the other is England’s women’s national football team, equally loved by my kids after their heroics in 2025. 

    But when you take a deeper look behind the Football Association and Hasbro deal, it starts to make perfect sense and tells us a lot about the power of partnerships. 

    The new character, Libby Lioness, will join the Peppa Pig universe ahead of the 2027 Women’s World Cup and is to be voiced by former England international Jill Scott. What’s more, the partnership will extend into YouTube content, toys, clothing and sporting accessories.

    It’s a brilliant way to bring the world of football into children’s lives, particularly girls’. It also shows how brands, broadcasters and the whole entertainment industry can play a role in building the next generation of fans. 

    Women’s sport in the UK hit a record 397m viewing hours in 2025, according to the Women’s Sport Trust. Deloitte also predicts global revenues in women’s sports will reach at least £2.2bn for the first time in 2026, up 25 per cent in a year. The growth of viewers means more brands are interested in sponsorship opportunities. 

    The commercial value is clear, but the biggest lesson for brands right now is not to wait until tournaments start to get in on the action.

    Peppa ultras and football fans offered a route into the other

    As the FA and Hasbro deal indicates, partnerships between women’s sports and brands should find ways to bring the game into everyday culture long before the first whistle blows. This helps generate momentum in fan audiences, building communities that converge around the sport at every level, without relying on live games to drum up a dedicated base. 

    People discover players through social media, follow their lives off-season, and rewatch match highlights on YouTube. This means that, for younger audiences, the relationship with sport can start well before they ever sit down to watch a full game. 

    Any brand can put its logo on a shirt or buy an ad slot around a fixture. But Hasbro shows brands that they can help tell the stories, create the content and build the experiences that make people care in the first place and, importantly, bring women’s football into conversations it might not reach otherwise. 

    My toddler doesn’t need to understand the offside rule to enjoy a story about a football character. And, since many parents are forced to watch Peppa Pig, combining the two makes football a shared family experience.  

    There are other great examples too, like when Google Pixel partnered with the FA to launch Pixel FC at the last Women’s World Cup. A group of women’s football creators and presenters made critical moments in the tournament accessible and opened up opportunities for girls and women in the game. 

    The best partnerships happen when two worlds with already strong narratives — in this case, Peppa ultras and football fans — give each a route into the other. 

    It’s a reminder that there’s no one way into women’s sport. Sometimes, it starts with a world-class performance. Sometimes it’s a player sharing a glimpse of life behind the scenes. And sometimes it’s a cartoon pig pulling on a football shirt.

    For much of the past decade and a half, describing the UK economy has been a relatively easy task. ‘Languid’ has often worked. ‘Stuttering’ has been another favourite. And when things have looked especially sullen, ‘moribund’ or ‘anaemic’ have more than sufficed.

    But if today’s GDP figures are anything to go by, then cliche-dependent hacks like this one might find themselves having to reach for their thesauruses in search of a new vernacular.

    Granted, a 0.1 per cent jump in economic activity in August is hardly cause to crack open the English sparkling wine. But it was, as almost every economist has been at pains to point out this morning, an expectation-defying 0.1 per cent nevertheless.

    The headwinds facing the upward nudge were manifold. And the sources of that resilience – improved productivity, early signs of a tech boom, and an uptick in our, yes, ‘moribund’ manufacturing sector – inspire some confidence.

    It is worth reflecting on why quite so many macro analysts are in such a celebratory mood. First, many had – quite understandably – expected the Middle East conflict, now stretching into its eighth month, to finally get its talons into business and consumer sentiment.

    Despite what Berenberg’s Andrew Wishart catchily frames as a “quadruple whammy” of rising taxes, higher energy prices, higher mortgage rates and a weak labour market, confidence has, in fact, been improving this year (albeit from a strikingly low ebb). And a look at consumer and services spending in today’s figures shows the trend has, again, defied expectations to the upside.

    Then there is the fact that August’s figure was going up against a tricky month-on-month comparative period. Boosted by spendthrift World Cup watchers, the UK economy grew by 0.4 per cent in both June and July, leading most economists to pencil in a minor contraction over the sleepier month of August.

    All of which means that over a three months, Britain’s once-languid economy has now grown by 0.7 per cent. It has also jumped 2.1 per cent over the past year, in what is our best 12 months since around 2017.

    “The UK’s resilience story continues,” Deutsche Bank’s Sanjay Raja said this morning. “It’s hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year.”

    The UK economy’s bleak midwinter

    And yet, because we can’t have nice things, there is, I’m afraid, a ‘but’. And that ‘but’ relates to what comes after what most think will be a solid end to the year.

    Early forecasts suggest that the start of 2027 could look a lot different from much of 2026. The Bank of England is all but nailed on to raise interest rates at its next meeting in November, with another 25 basis-point hike expected in early 2027. That alone will considerably shift households’ breathing space – and with no end of the inflationary Iran war in sight – price pressure remains uncomfortably hot; especially with the economy chugging along as healthily as it is.

    Even more ominous is the direction of energy prices, which are due to build up a head of steam at the start of next year. By the Bank of England’s reckoning, households can expect their energy bills to jump by some 20 per cent in January. That, in turn, will help carry inflation to four per cent, double the monetary authority’s two per cent target. All the while, improvement in people’s pay is expected to slow.

    “The combination of rising inflation and slowing wage growth is a toxic mix for households’ real income growth,” says RSM UK’s Thomas Pugh.

    Then again, people much cleverer than me have been predicting a sharp economic downturn for much of this year – and it hasn’t materialised. But with so many competing headwinds, overwhelming consensus is we can only be so resilient. Journalists’ thesauruses appear safe… for now.

    Standing in the teeny tiny, Netflix-Christmas-film-coded courtyard outside Cloth Cornhill, I feel sad. This opening drills the final nail in the coffin of the former Simpsons Tavern, the capital’s oldest chophouse, which was on this site since 1757.

    Everyone’s got a story about whose fault it is that that chophouse closed. Rumours range from the former tenants being massively overdue rental payments before the pandemic, through to it being the greedy landlord’s fault. Either way, the former manager is bitter that in 2022, his run came to an end – he said this in a lengthy LinkedIn post – and rightly so: he was the final custodian of the Simpsons Tavern brand, which had been in place for 250 years.

    In the drizzle, my colleague and I spend 45 minutes admiring the expensive, shiny refurbishment. Nursing pints of ale, we discuss the whole sorry situation. Despite my empathy for the old guard, who still retain the rights to the Simpsons Tavern name and plan to open somewhere else in the “spirit” of Simpsons, it makes for tantalising gossip. I’d love to know what went down, but the landlord is uncontactable. It’s impossible not to feel that the fallout is one big shame. RIP Simpsons Tavern, for now, anyway.

    But today, we’re talking about Cloth Cornhill. Founders Ben Butterworth, Joe Haynes and Tom Hurst have recreated the old place as if it were 1757 again. The landlords were so scrupulous, they asked to see sample menus before they’d agree to hand over the keys, so this trio must be, at the very least, charismatic. Just don’t say that anything is in homage to the old venue or ‘bringing anything back’ as that gets them in murky legal waters.

    Cloth Cornhill: how about a ‘pie course’?

    Its gleaming mahogany high-backed benches have been buffered to within an inch of their lives, the pub reorganised so the feng shui is better – that’s a fancy way of saying it’s easier to get to the bar – and to give more emphasis to the building’s features, such as the front bay window. Period wooden floor replaces lino; two part-time workers spent six months polishing 22 faux vintage brass lamps.

    On autumn’s first sodden Monday, the place is heaving. If the brief was to recreate a cacophonous Dickensian tavern, consider that met. Only there are also quiet contemporary enhancements, such as sound dampening added to the ceiling so you can actually have a conversation. One lonely photo of a barmaid with two cakes in front of her boobs hangs upstairs as a reminder of the good old days. I’m told some of the waitresses used to show their breasts if they got tipped enough, and many from the Simpson’s Tavern days have returned after the reopening (I can’t promise they were the ones flashing the customers however).

    Former patrons have even demanded the old menu back. Is it pastiche? A little bit. How can it not be? But in 10 years, when the old guard have all died, no one will remember Simpsons Tavern anyway, they’ll just say there’s a really cool old school chophouse called Cloth Cornhill. Such is life.

    Prepare your gout stool

    As for the food, Victorian gentlemen would be preparing their gout stools. The menu features superlative spins on British comfort food. To kick off, devils on horseback (prunes filled with black pudding and wrapped in bacon) were just divine – dense enough to suck like boiled sweets. ‘Sausage on the side’ with mustard is delicious, the meat both course and smooth (a version of this dish was on the former Simpsons menu, although the owners insist it was inspired by a recipe in a book found during the refit).

    We are recommended the ‘pie course’, which is the most hedonistic thing I have ever heard. I decide on venison, bacon and prune, with pastry that was nine tenths butter, and it is obviously banging, a reflection of Hurst’s philosophy: locally sourced meat, diligently cooked and married with the odd unusual ingredient.

    We drink loads of booze to induce more hunger, plus we’re at Simpsons Tavern – sorry, Cloth Cornhill – and that’s what you do in here. “This place was known for gout production,” says our waiter, which I think was supposed to make us feel better about over-ordering. The sommelier brings over something from the Southern Rhone to follow a funky rose that tasted like overripe strawberries.

    The Big Four have collectively secured over £1.5bn in public contracts so far this year despite the UK government’s pledge to cut spending on external consultants to save taxpayers’ money.

    An investigation by market intelligence platform Tussell found the government has awarded KPMG, Deloitte, EY and PwC over £1.5bn in contracts so far in 2026, more than the entirety of 2025, which stood at £1.04bn.

    The data showed it was the second most successful calendar year for the Big Four since Tussell began recording in 2012, beaten only by contracting during the height of the pandemic in 2020.

    Leading the Big Four, Deloitte secured £650m across 108 contracts this year. The bulk of these wins focused on IT services, digital transformation, and data analytics. Home Office IT spending accounted for the majority of this new work, including a standout £200m contract for Home Office Digital’s Data Services and Analytics (DSA) unit.

    KPMG and EY won the largest contract, worth £456m, awarded by the Cabinet Office, which covers training for civil servants over the next two years.

    In terms of rankings, despite being the smallest compared to its competitors, KPMG took second place, winning over £413m in government contract work. EY was third, with an overall value of £260m booked so far this year. Despite being the largest, PwC often takes a proportionally smaller share of public sector work than its rivals. It ranked fourth with over £211m.

    As the consultancy market tightens due to the influx of AI and private-sector pulling back on external spending due to an economic downturn, government work remains resilient for firms.

    Tamzen Isacsson, chief executive of the Management Consultancies Association (MCA), told City AM: “Consultants are playing a vital role in helping government improve public services for taxpayers, and their specialist expertise is in demand in areas such as digital transformation, cybersecurity, AI and organisational change.”

    Civil service skills gap challenge

    The increase in UK government spending comes after Labour pledged in 2024 to slash taxpayer spending on external consultants.

    The government unveiled plans for greater procurement control in November 2024, rolling out a framework to save £1.2bn by 2026 by freezing non-essential consultancy hires and targeting a 50 per cent spend reduction in the years to follow.

    However, the government’s biggest challenge is the civil service skills shortage, especially during digital transformation.

    Emma Carroll, principal consultant at Source Global Research, told City AM: “Often, consultants are brought in to tackle the most complex projects where specific expertise is needed and where there is a lack of internal talent, and there are some prime examples of this at play at the moment, including cybersecurity, technology implementation (including AI), or data readiness work, where the government simply can’t risk falling behind.

    “The defence sector has also been a critical area of focus for the UK government this year, and consulting support has been and will continue to be important here,” she added.

    Source predicts the UK public sector consulting market will grow by around five per cent in 2026, versus around six per cent for the wider consulting market.

    Isacsson added: “We recognise the fiscal pressures facing government and share its ambition to improve productivity and delivery across the public sector. Effective use of consultancy helps government do more with less, bringing in specialist expertise where it is needed, supporting innovation, and building capability inside the civil service for the future.”

    The Cabinet Office was contacted for comment.

    A public art piece appearing to satirise the process of quantitative easing this week popped up outside the Bank of England. Initial claims that the piece was a Banksy were quickly poohpoohed, primarily due to the sculpture’s perceived quality. “This has Goldsmiths MFA student written all over it,” disparaged one observer on Reddit, to which another replied that did not rule out Banksy entirely. The City of London Corporation for its part has said the origins of the piece are unknown, but nevertheless wasted no time in putting up big barriers around it for the sake of “public safety”.

    HASTY HIRING

    About three months into the Burnham premiership and things are still in flux. Advisers who had been working under Starmer were given three-month probation periods to prove their worth. Now Burnham is looking to further strengthen his policy unit with new hires in three areas: ‘Growth & Macroeconomics’, ‘Public Control’, and ‘Work, Social Security & Pensions’.     So far, Sadiq Khan’s only transport achievements have been to cut the ribbon on new projects that his predecessors started, writes James Ford

    In recent weeks there has been a flurry of activity regarding London’s pipeline of proposed new transport infrastructure projects. Transport for London (TfL) is finally running a public consultation on the West London Orbital rail project. A laundry list of transport projects has been touted in the Evening Standard, presumably with TfL’s connivance. And the results of a previous consultation on the DLR extension to Thamesmead have been made public, showing significant popular support. Should we conclude that London is finally getting the infrastructure it needs? Of course not.

    Rather than a feeling of excitement about new lines and new stations, the correct response you should have is a profound sense of déjà vu. The four grands projets at the top of TfL’s pipeline – Crossrail 2, the West London Orbital, the DLR extension and the Bakerloo Line extension – have all been on TfL’s to-do list since well before 2016, when this Mayor assumed office. Worse still, the biggest project (Crossrail 2) has been mothballed since November 2020. The earliest that it could open is the 2050s.

    The sad truth is that this ‘new’ activity is all stuff that a good Mayor of London would have done in their first year in office, not their tenth. And, if you somehow forgot to start campaigning for all this investment and infrastructure in your first year (or even your first term), then Sadiq Khan had a rare second chance to set the ball rolling in the summer of 2022 when the Elizabeth Line opened. In that moment London swooned with excitement about how this Tube line had delivered beautiful stations, faster journey times and new connections. Londoners flocked to the new line in huge numbers and TfL’s coffers overflowed with extra fares income. That would have been a good time to announce that London’s next big project – whichever one it was – had got the green light.

    But no, it seems that City Hall and TfL are only now slowly creaking into gear to deliver the infrastructure that London needed in 2016. This decade of delay means that these projects are all set to cost more to build. In 2016, Crossrail 2 was set to cost £32.6bn. By 2019 costs had spiralled to $41.3bn. Now it is thought to cost an estimated £45bn. Between 2020 and 2026 alone the cost of the DLR extension doubled.

    What has Sadiq Khan achieved in transport?

    In the decade since 2016, the economic and political situation has deteriorated. The government’s focus is on the north, not London. It has signalled support for the £45bn Northern Powerhouse Rail scheme but has so far refused to commit to chip in towards the £1.7bn cost of the DLR extension. At the same time, TfL’s ability to fund this project from its own funds has declined. TfL was carrying debt of £9.1bn in 2016 but £13.9bn in 2026, making it currently the most indebted local authority body in the UK. The second most indebted local authority in the UK? Well, that’s City Hall of course, with £4.7bn of debt.

    So far, Khan’s only transport achievements have been to cut the ribbon on new projects that his predecessors started. The Elizabeth Line was approved under Ken Livingstone in 2007 and broke ground under Boris Johnson in 2009. The Northern Line extension to Battersea was greenlit two years before Khan was elected. And Boris also approved the Overground extension to Barking Riverside a few months before he left office.

    I, for one, am glad that these vital infrastructure projects are no longer stuck in limbo. But we do have to reflect on what this lost decade has cost London. This sudden, dramatic burst of activity by City Hall and TfL may seem like progress but it is a sad, desperate race for a meaningful legacy from a mayor that is all too aware he is running out of time.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

]]> Agility’s 284-pound Digit 5 runs for 90 minutes and recharges in nine, a 10-to-1 work-to-charge ratio the company says can deliver more than 20 productive hours a day, with early customer access planned for the first half of 2027 https://siliconcanals.com/n-agilitys-284-pound-digit-5-runs-for-90-minutes-and-recharges-in-nine-a-10-to-1-work-to-charge-ratio-the-company-says-can-deliver-more-than-20-productive-hours-a-day-with-early-customer-access/ Mon, 21 Sep 2026 19:00:38 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109721

Agility says Digit 5 is engineered for unfenced work near people; its runtime, charging and daily-productivity figures remain manufacturer specifications ahead of planned 2027 customer access.]]>

Correction, 1 October 2026: An earlier version miscounted the number of charge cycles in a 24-hour day and said early access was more than a year away. The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

What a 20-hour day actually means

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. The one field metric that has been independently reported involves the previous generation, not Digit 5: at a GXO logistics facility, Digit 4 reportedly 98% accuracy sorting totes over more than 100,000 units, a real operational number — though it speaks to picking accuracy, a separate metric from hours worked per day.

Heavier lifts, taller reach than the last generation

Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. The robot can repeatedly lift loads of up to 50 pounds, which the company describes as a 40 percent jump over Digit 4’s payload, and it can reach items up to 7.2 feet high, up from about 5.5 feet on the previous version, according to Forbes’ coverage of the launch. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing. Vinted makes its money almost entirely from the buyer’s side of the transaction: a fixed fee of roughly $0.70 plus a variable fee of about 5 percent of the item’s price, charged in the buyer’s local currency (figures as of late 2025) — according to Vinted’s own Buyer Protection fee page. An hour disappears into the phone and the honest inventory afterwards runs to three items: a man cutting marble, somebody’s strong opinion about interest rates, a dog on a skateboard.

None of it is retained in any way worth having. The hour still lands like work.

That mismatch, between the feeling of effort and the absence of anything learned, has a reasonable research explanation behind it, and willpower barely features in it.

A feed is a run of cold starts

Reading a book is one long continuous job. The brain loads a setting, a cast, an argument, and then keeps using that same setup for as long as the reading lasts.

A feed offers nothing of the kind.

Each post arrives with its own subject, tone, format and rules, which means the machinery of attention has to reconfigure itself before any of the content can be processed.

A feed adds another recurring job: a verdict. Each item has to be sized up for whether it is true, whether it is funny, whether it is aimed at anyone in particular. That call gets made before the thing can be dismissed, and then made again at the next one, and the one after that.

Psychologists have taken that reconfiguration apart. In a paper published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans described two stages: goal shifting, meaning the decision to do this now instead of that, and rule activation, meaning the swap of mental instructions from the old job to the new one. Both stages take time. A single switch might cost only a few tenths of a second. That sounds trivial until you count the switches inside an hour of scrolling.

Their experiments used arithmetic and shape-sorting rather than phones, so applying the finding to a feed is an inference, not a measurement.

The part that stays behind

Switching also leaves something on the floor. Sophie Leroy, now a professor at the University of Washington Bothell, coined the term attention residue in a 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, after experiments in which people were pulled off one task and pushed onto another. Performance on the second task dropped, because a slice of their attention was still parked on the first, and the effect was sharpest when the first task had been left unfinished.

Scrolling has the shape of that setup. Post after post is dropped mid-thought and replaced by the next one, which looks a great deal like the unfinished condition Leroy identified as the costly one. Her participants were working through lab tasks, though. The parallel to a phone is drawn by analogy, and nobody has run the experiment there.

Forty-seven seconds

Gloria Mark, a professor of informatics at the University of California, Irvine, has been logging how long people stay on a single screen since 2004. Back then the average was about two and a half minutes. In an interview with the University of California, she put the recent figure at roughly 47 seconds, with a median of 40, meaning half of all observed stretches were shorter than that.

That number needs handling with care. It is assembled from separate studies across two decades, not one group of people followed the whole way, and what it measures is screen behaviour. People still read long books. They just do it somewhere other than a browser tab.

Why a book behaves differently

Does the medium itself change how much gets understood? Pablo Delgado of the University of Valencia and three co-authors pooled 54 studies covering more than 171,000 participants in a meta-analysis for Educational Research Review, and found a consistent, modest advantage for paper. The gap widened when reading was timed instead of self-paced, held for informational texts but not narrative ones, and grew across the years studied, an unhelpful trend for anyone expecting digital natives to close it.

Pooling dozens of experiments makes that result sturdier than any single study, though the effect itself stays small.

Maryanne Wolf, who studies the reading brain at UCLA, argues in an op-ed for the Guardian that skimming squeezes out the slower processes that make reading useful: drawing inferences, making analogies, testing whether a claim is true, stepping into another person’s point of view. Move the eye fast enough and there is no room left for any of it.

Where the tiredness comes from

Fatigue needs its own explanation, and it comes from a separate strand of Mark’s research.

In a study presented at the 2008 CHI conference, Mark, working with Daniela Gudith and Ulrich Klocke, interrupted people mid-task and measured what happened. The interrupted group finished faster, with no drop in quality, which was the surprise. They also reported more stress, more frustration, more time pressure and more effort.

Compensation, in other words.

The brain appears to cover the cost of fragmentation by spending harder. Mark’s participants were working rather than scrolling, and the equivalent test has not been run on a feed, so the link is suggestive rather than established. Even so, the flatness and irritability at the end of a long scroll, the vague sense of having been mugged, match what those participants described.

Which puts the whole exercise in a different light. An hour on a feed involves several hundred small decisions made at speed, each one demanding a quick ruling on what the thing is and whether it matters. The content was the least of it. The deciding was the job.

Nobody sends an invoice for that. The tiredness is the receipt.

A pair of speakers, two years old, is up for sale online. When no music is playing, they give off an annoying static noise, and the listing does not say so.

A buyer’s message ends with a pointed question: “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” In one of the experiments built around that exact question, 85 percent of sellers mentioned the noise, and fewer buyers than that expected their seller to mention a problem.

Shira Garber and three colleagues staged a string of these secondhand sales online across five main studies and a pilot, added a second pilot that surveyed people about what drives negotiators, and reported the results in an open-access paper in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin this July. Buyers, they found, often underestimated how honest sellers would be. Sellers also reported more concern with being honest, fair and kind, and less concern with the money, than buyers credited them with.

How often did sellers come clean?

In each of the five main studies, some participants played sellers of a secondhand device with a defect they had been told about: an iPod whose battery drained fast, an electric scooter with a faulty battery, the speakers with the static. The rest played buyers, who could earn bonuses for accurately predicting how honest sellers would be.

In the first four studies, a seller counted as honest only if a reply named the defect. Staying quiet counted as dishonest, and so did a dodge like a battery that “isn’t brand new.”

The first pilot set the pattern. Of 76 online workers playing sellers, 63.2 percent picked a truthful opening message over one describing the iPod as being in excellent condition. Of 85 observers given the same information, 43.5 percent predicted the truthful one.

In Study 1, the 176 sellers wrote their own replies to “What can you tell me about it?” and “Anything else?” Of those sellers, 51.7 percent disclosed the battery problem, while the 270 buyers guessed, on average, that 43.2 percent would. With the scooter and a direct question in Study 2, three quarters of sellers disclosed the fault.

The rate swung with the setup. One cause, a direct question, got its own test; other swings the researchers could not fully explain. Until the last study, the exchanges were also largely scripted, with sellers answering pre-written buyer messages rather than a live counterpart.

Study 3, with 483 participants, gave half the sellers the pointed “The speakers don’t have any problems, do they?” and half the open “What can you tell me about them?” Buyers here were not told about the static, which is closer to how a real listing works.

The direct question made sellers more likely to mention the noise. Buyers’ predictions did not move with it.

The gap between expected and actual honesty was statistically significant under the direct question and not under the open one, so even inside this paper it did not show up everywhere. Of several possible reasons Study 1 still found a gap with open questions, the authors single out one: sellers there had two chances to come clean, and concealing twice may weigh more on a seller’s conscience than concealing once.

Study 5 was the only one that paired people live. It matched 422 participants into 211 buyer-seller pairs on an online platform, and some pairs first spent three minutes chatting about something they had enjoyed recently or how they unwind after a busy day.

Plain caution, a buyer bracing for the worst to avoid a loss, gets mixed treatment: the Study 4 discussion offers it as a possible added force, while the general discussion says it cannot explain the results, because in the first pilot observers with nothing at stake still underestimated the sellers.

Their mediation analyses deserve a lighter touch than the abstract’s sentence suggests. Buyers and sellers answered parallel versions of the motive questions rather than the same ones, and the authors say the results should be “cautiously interpreted” for that reason. Sellers rated their motives after choosing whether to disclose, which leaves room for a flattering story told afterward, though the authors argue buyers’ parallel ratings may reduce that concern. And in Study 1, the measure of anticipated guilt and related feelings showed no significant difference between buyers and sellers.

Small stakes, narrow scope

The stakes stayed small. Most bonuses were paid by lottery, and a seller in Study 1 had a five percent chance of earning at most $7. The authors grant that low stakes may keep self-interest from fully switching on, while citing earlier work that finds self-interest at work even when stakes are small.

The honesty studied was one kind: telling a buyer about a defect the seller knew. Misrepresenting a bottom price or inventing urgency, both named by the authors, were outside the design. They describe the findings as “based primarily on Western participant samples,” and the sales were one-off exchanges between strangers, chosen to keep reputation largely out of play. Ongoing work relationships and repeat customers sit outside what was measured.

Suspicion is sometimes the sensible response, and the paper says so. A buyer facing a salesperson expected to use persuasion tactics, or shopping where one side knows far more than the other, as with used cars, has good reason for care. The paper does not argue for trusting everyone. It asks for work on when doubting a counterpart’s honesty hurts a negotiator and when it protects one.

Every finding in this piece comes from the published text and tables of one paper, read by an editorial desk that reports on research and does not train negotiators; the supplementary files the paper points to could not be opened. The studies compared predictions with replies across hundreds of people, which says something about buyers and sellers like the ones studied, taken as groups, and cannot tell anyone whether the particular seller in their inbox is being straight with them. For a purchase that matters, sensible safeguards include an independent inspection, a written description of the item’s condition, and the buyer protection some platforms offer.

This paper did not measure what the gap costs. The authors’ illustration is a used car that looks too good to be true, and a buyer who distrusts the seller, walks away, and settles for something worse. Examining what the honesty gap does to the outcomes of negotiations is what they call an important next step; they also call for testing the idea where far more money is at stake.
