]]> Europe is an attractive place to live because of its high quality of life, job opportunities, and stability. However, attracting people to live here for the lifestyle is different from attracting talent and companies to move here and build.

The latter entails companies bringing teams with them, hiring locally, and establishing R&D that fosters an entrepreneurial ecosystem that benefits the continent as a whole. This is an area that Europe isn’t doing so well in, especially compared to the US.

The trend shows that approximately 10% of EU scale-ups relocate abroad, with around 85% moving to the United States. Furthermore, between 2008-2021, nearly 30% of unicorns moved their headquarters abroad (again, mostly to the US). 

Despite this, the narrative has recently been disrupted by Langdock, a Berlin-based AI startup. They moved their parent company from the US to Germany and aim to become a “European hyperscaler”.

This illustrates that the phenomenon of startups relocating to the US from Europe isn’t set in stone. Europe can attract and retain its talent. This article explores different cases of that and explores how to get teams to build here rather than just use Europe as a stepping stone.

The US or Europe: How do startups choose?

It is imperative to understand Europe’s main competitor in order to learn where more can be done. The US isn’t just where most European startups relocate, it also captures 85% of startups worldwide. If there’s a US VC, chances are the startup will relocate there. In fact, a Delaware parent company, a US-based legal entity that owns and controls the startup’s operations, including those in Europe, is frequently a precondition US venture funds set before they’ll invest.

Then comes the fact that the US grants access to a single market compared to Europe’s 27 member states. Buyers spread across European jurisdictions take longer to close than buyers spread across US states operating under one framework. This forces European startups to cross borders earlier than many of their US counterparts (something the EU. Inc Framework is working to address). Still, 97% moves are partial exits, with companies retaining operations in their home country. Only around three-quarters of relocating CEOs physically move to the new destination.

The capital gap between Europe and the US cannot be ignored either. Contrary to popular sentiment that the US is more forgiving towards founders whose previous enterprises have failed and that they have more appetite for risk, the reality is that there is more capital to go around to fund newer attempts (€930 billion versus €150 billion in the EU, around sixfold to be precise). European investors are understandably more cautious due to this.

Having prefaced the US’s attraction for startups, how do cases like Langdock exist?

Langdock’s move was commercial. Their customers’ legal teams kept flagging the US parent company as a data-risk exposure despite the fact that it had no staff, servers, or systems access. The US Cloud Act in particular was a great cause of concern.

80% of the company was owned by founders and employees living in the EU, and the teams, coupled with approximately 13,000 client organisations, were being served from Germany.

In short, everything was already based in Europe, but the parent company was created to initially attract US investors and benefit from the start-up accelerator Y Combinator.

What Europe has been doing and what it should do instead

Europe has acted as a magnet for talent to study, train, and build. However, its retention of that same talent has proven to be less successful, as discussed previously. The focus has mostly been on easing restrictions that bring talent into the country, namely by putting in special visa schemes. That is not to say that they haven’t been successful at that.

Germany issued 72% of the EU’s Blue Cards in 2024, which fast-tracks skilled workers residing in the EU. France’s Tech Visa provides a simplified residence route for startup employees, and 1200 companies have utilised it for international recruitment since the program was launched. Portugal’s Digital Nomad Visa (D8) was launched in 2022 to attract remote workers without needing a Portuguese employer or company. It has approved 7,664 applications since then. 

But talent attraction is not only about how many people move to Europe. It makes a positive impact only when people and companies build teams, hire locally, create R&D capacity, and stay long enough to strengthen the ecosystem. While founders and talented people moving for lifestyle reasons is good, it is not the same as a company bringing sales teams, engineering, and creating jobs in the area. The good part is that there are already some examples where the latter is happening. 

Unicorn Factory Lisbon is one such example. Launched in 2022, has attracted 82 technology companies to set up offices in the city, creating more than 16,000 jobs.

Such clusters are important because their alumni can go on to become new founders, as seen in the case of Talkdesk and OutSystems alumni, who founded Speak, Cleverly.ai, and Screenloop.

Barcelona serves as a stronger example where 6 unicorns are headquartered in the city, and create €36 billion in combined enterprise value by locally-based companies. Whether Lisbon can transform from simply attracting branches and teams to headquarters remains to be seen. 

Estonia has provided another innovative way of attracting companies. By providing individual e-residencies, it allows global entrepreneurs to register a business online, access the EU market, and enjoy a 0% corporate tax rate on reinvested and retained profits. This has resulted in dividends amounting to €124.9 million for the country. 

The Next Stage for Europe’s Talent

Europe has proven that it is quite capable of attracting talent, but it has yet to stem the loss of its talent to other countries, especially the US. Different symptoms have to be addressed differently.

For example, incentivising companies to open their branches and headquarters on the continent. Providing a common framework for countries to operate with. The issues with capital cannot be ignored. Europe’s pension funds can compensate for the discrepancy to an extent. Europe has proven its innovativeness, but it is time to build it.

]]> “Dear Europe, why are you killing EU Inc?” That’s how many in the European startup community were greeted when they read this morning’s brief by the highly supported EU–INC initiative.

Backed by some of Europe’s most prominent startup founders and investors, the initiative has issued an urgent warning that the European Union’s proposed ‘EU Inc’ pan-European company framework is losing the very provisions that made it attractive to entrepreneurs.

In a public statement released on 15 October 2026, the campaign accused European policymakers of weakening the proposal through months of negotiations, reducing an ambitious effort to little more than a fast-track company registration system.

Since launch, the EU-INC campaign has since attracted more than 26,000 supporters from across 27 countries, including founders associated with Stripe, Mistral AI, Klarna and Wise, alongside investors from Atomico, Index Ventures and Seedcamp. Its central ambition has been to establish a common European company structure that would help startups access international investment, recruit talent and expand across borders without navigating fragmented national corporate systems.

In its latest statement, addressed directly to Europe’s Heads of State and Government, EU–INC declared: “The EU Inc you championed – one that will enable Europe to compete at scale – no longer exists. Months of negotiations have removed the core of the proposal. As it stands, it will do nothing to improve Europe’s competitiveness.”

The initiative has not been formally cancelled, and negotiations remain ongoing. However, campaigners argue that the emerging compromises threaten to undermine its original purpose.

From European dream to compromise

Known as the 28th regime, EU Inc was introduced by the European Commission on 18 March 2026 as an optional corporate framework operating alongside the 27 existing national systems.

The Commission’s original proposal would allow entrepreneurs to establish a company digitally within 48 hours for no more than €100, without minimum share capital requirements. It also envisaged simplified share transfers, digital insolvency procedures, access to modern financing instruments and a common employee stock option scheme with deferred taxation.

One of its central elements was freedom to choose the EU country in which a business incorporates, regardless of where its employees and operations are based. This would allow companies and investors to converge around familiar legal jurisdictions and standardised investment documentation, similar to the role Delaware plays in the United States.

The EU–INC campaign argues that restrictions on this freedom would prevent a recognised European corporate standard from emerging.

Stock options on the chopping block

Another major disagreement concerns employee stock options, which startups frequently use to attract skilled workers when they cannot match the salaries offered by larger companies.

The Commission originally proposed a harmonised framework under which taxation would be deferred until employees sold their shares, avoiding situations where workers face tax liabilities before receiving any proceeds.

However, the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU introduced restrictions in its July compromise text, limiting the proposed stock option scheme to companies with fewer than 1,000 employees and turnover below €450 million. Subsequent negotiations have raised further questions about whether the provisions will survive at all.

According to Agence Europe, discussions among EU ambassadors on 30 September failed to resolve disagreements over stock option taxation.

Stéphane Séjourné, European Commissioner responsible for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, had already warned against weakening the framework during a meeting of industry ministers in Brussels on 24 September.

Séjourné said: “I cannot see the 28th regime and the Commission’s proposal without stock option harmonisation.”

The proposed central digital company register has also become a point of contention. The Commission initially envisaged an EU-level registration interface followed by a central register, designed to make company information accessible across Member States and simplify procedures such as opening bank accounts, verifying ownership and conducting compliance checks.

Yet the first Council compromise text removed plans for the central register, prompting criticism from campaigners who consider a shared digital infrastructure essential to establishing trust in the new corporate framework.

Workers’ rights enter the fray

Beyond these disagreements, EU Inc has encountered opposition from European trade unions concerned about its potential impact on workers’ rights.

On 24 September, hundreds of trade union activists demonstrated in Brussels, arguing that the proposed framework could enable companies to register in countries with less demanding corporate rules while operating elsewhere.

The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) has warned of potential risks to collective bargaining, employee representation and national labour protections.

The Commission maintains that EU Inc. would not override national employment and social legislation. EU–INC emphasised that workers would remain protected by the labour laws of the countries where they work, while companies and employees would continue to pay taxes according to applicable national rules.

Taxation represents another unresolved dimension. In July 2026, the European Parliament adopted recommendations for an optional tax regime accompanying EU Inc, including a single EU VAT number, centralised VAT declarations and refunds, and simplified corporate tax procedures.

This leaves open questions about how much administrative friction EU Inc would actually remove for businesses operating across multiple European markets.

A make-or-break moment for Europe

The dispute comes at a sensitive moment for European competitiveness. The EU has repeatedly identified fragmented regulation, limited access to growth capital and difficulties retaining entrepreneurial talent as barriers to building globally competitive technology companies.

With EU institutions targeting a political agreement before the end of 2026, the coming negotiations will determine how much of the Commission’s original proposal survives.

EU–INC is now appealing directly to Europe’s national leaders to intervene, reverse objections to its central provisions and restore what it considers the minimum requirements for a functioning European startup standard.

“If Europe’s leaders cannot even align on a solution like EU Inc, Europe’s founders will lose more than a proposal. They will lose faith in Europe’s ability to face the challenges of our time. Europe’s founders will have a future. Whether that future is European is in your hands.”

]]> NVIDIA has had a busy week on this side of the pond.

From announcing new investments in British and French startups to launching collaborations in Sweden, supporting AI research and bringing developers together in Barcelona, Paris and London, the US chipmaker appears determined to play a bigger role in the continent’s technological future.

The activity comes ahead of NVIDIA GTC Berlin, taking place from 20 to 22 October 2026, where founder and CEO Jensen Huang will deliver a keynote.

But beyond the conference preparations, the announcements reveal a wider strategy involving startup funding, computing infrastructure, research partnerships and the development of AI applications across European industries.

NVIDIA’s 2026 European investment trail

This week builds on an investment footprint already documented by EU-Startups throughout 2026. The company has participated in funding rounds involving French AI developers Mistral AI (€3 billion) and AMI (€890 million), alongside British companies Nscale (€1.7 billion), Wayve (€1 billion), Ineffable Intelligence (€937 million) and Orbital Industries (€43 million).

In Spain, Valencia-based iPronics secured €107.6 million with NVIDIA backing, while its venture arm, NVentures, joined a €42 million extension for Sweden’s Legora.

Together, these eight announcements represent approximately €7.72 billion in company financing, although NVIDIA’s individual contributions have not been disclosed. Earlier investments in British startup PhysicsX and France’s Scintil Photonics further illustrate its established involvement in European AI development.

Fresh bets on British and French startups

Continuing this investment commitment in Europe, NVIDIA unveiled planned investments in five startups: Boltz, Foresight, Hiverge, Prima Mente and Riverlane. Although the individual investment amounts have not been disclosed, the selection of companies provides an indication of where NVIDIA sees opportunities for technological development.

These companies join NVIDIA’s existing investment activity in the UK, where it has previously supported startups including Synthesia, Wayve, Basecamp Research and Ineffable Intelligence.

The announcement also highlighted the role of NVIDIA’s Inception programme, which now includes more than 3,100 UK companies. The programme provides eligible startups with access to technical resources, expertise and opportunities to connect with NVIDIA’s wider network.

Across the English Channel, NVIDIA announced planned minority investments in four French startups: Doctolib, Entalpic, Genesis AI and Pigment. As previously reported by EU-Startups.

On 13 October, Huang attended an AI ecosystem reception in Paris alongside founders, researchers and policymakers, including France’s Minister of the Economy, Roland Lescure. Later that evening, he met President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace to discuss AI infrastructure, investments in French technology companies, open-source development and AI safety.

Speaking at the Paris reception, Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA, said, “Europe is one of the great regions of industrial manufacturing,” adding, “This is the beginning of the AI journey for the EU.”

This week also saw the launch of the Startup Ireland AI Accelerator Programme, which aims to support 1,000 new startups by 2030. NVIDIA is among the technology partners associated with the initiative, further extending its involvement in Europe’s entrepreneurship networks.

Sweden’s AI ambitions take shape

Beyond France and the UK, the Nordics have emerged as another focus of NVIDIA’s European activities. The company highlighted how startups and technology companies across the region are building products using its computing platforms and open models. With several companies demonstrating applications ranging from intellectual property management to autonomous transportation.

Stockholm-based Stilta is using NVIDIA’s Nemotron models to analyse patent portfolios, helping businesses monitor intellectual property across large numbers of patents. Agaton is applying similar technology to real-time sales intelligence, while Swedish speech technology company Klang has developed Pianissimo, a transcription model trained on more than 50,000 hours of Swedish speech.

Meanwhile, Gothenburg-based Embedl, a member of NVIDIA Inception, has collaborated with Space Cargo Unlimited to develop an onboard AI prototype that monitors protein crystallisation experiments in space without requiring continuous connectivity to Earth.

Perhaps one of the most interesting Nordic announcements for founders was NVIDIA’s collaboration with the Norrsken Foundation to establish the Stockholm AI Lab.

Scheduled to open in 2027, the new hub will bring together AI-focused entrepreneurs working on challenges in healthcare, climate, food and society. Located in central Stockholm, it will also house NVIDIA’s local office, bringing the company physically closer to entrepreneurs developing AI technologies.

Another important development comes from Sweden AI Factory, one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories, which announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to startups and SMEs.

The expansion of AI infrastructure across the Nordics is also gathering pace. NVIDIA reports that regional cloud providers are working towards approximately one gigawatt of AI cloud capacity by the end of 2027, with companies including Nscale, Verda and Volta among those participating in the expansion.

“Physical AI is the next big opportunity,” said Deepu Talla, vice president of robotics and edge computing at NVIDIA. “Around 70% of GDP is in the physical world, and that makes physical AI one of the largest opportunities ahead of us. Europe can combine AI with its human capital, engineering expertise and industrial capabilities to create more value.”

Europe’s AI opportunity comes with a catch

Taken together, this week’s announcements suggest that NVIDIA’s strategy in Europe extends well beyond financial investments.

By supporting startups, offering access to computing resources, collaborating with research institutions and establishing closer relationships with developer communities, NVIDIA is positioning itself across multiple stages of the European AI development process.

At the same time, NVIDIA’s expansion raises questions about Europe’s technological independence. While access to funding, computing infrastructure and technical expertise could help European startups compete internationally, greater adoption of NVIDIA’s technology could also increase their dependence on a single US supplier.

The bigger question is whether Europe’s startups can use this momentum to build lasting, globally competitive companies of their own. If they succeed, NVIDIA could benefit from supplying the infrastructure behind their growth, while European founders have an opportunity to capture more of the value created by the next generation of AI technologies.

]]> As artificial intelligence reshapes how companies build, test and operate software, it is also transforming the cybersecurity landscape, leaving many organisations struggling to keep pace with emerging threats.

Recent research from AI Score, examining UK-based organisations across the public and private sectors, found that 31% had experienced an AI-related incident or near miss in the past two years. Among those reporting incidents, 44% said confidential or sensitive data had been entered into an AI tool.

Despite these risks, 92% of organisations are already using AI beyond the pilot stage, while significant gaps remain in their ability to identify, monitor and control its use.

AI-powered phishing, automated attacks and increasingly sophisticated impersonation techniques are creating new cybersecurity challenges. At the same time, the rapid adoption of AI agents, autonomous systems and AI-assisted software development is introducing additional vulnerabilities that traditional security tools may struggle to address.

Across Europe, a growing number of startups are developing solutions to tackle these emerging threats. Some are building tools to protect AI agents and connected systems from exploitation, while others are leveraging AI to automate penetration testing, improve threat detection and accelerate security investigations.

From securing AI-powered systems to using the technology to strengthen cyber defences, these 10 European startups are tackling the next generation of cybersecurity challenges as both attackers and defenders increasingly turn to artificial intelligence.

Cytix (UK)

Founded in 2020, UK cybersecurity startup Cytix is tackling the risks created by AI-driven software change. In August 2026, the company raised €6 million in a Series A to tackle the problems created by rapid software change.

The company argues that AI-assisted development, agentic workflows and continuous delivery are outpacing traditional security models. Its platform is designed to help organisations manage security risk as software changes more quickly and more frequently.

Escape (France)

Founded in 2020, French startup Escape is developing an AI-powered offensive security engineering platform.

In March 2026, the company raised €15.4 million in a Series A round led by Balderton. Its work is part of a broader shift towards continuous, automated offensive security, where organisations use AI-assisted testing to identify vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

Exein (Italy)

Founded in 2018, Italian embedded cybersecurity company Exein is developing technology to protect connected devices, autonomous systems and physical AI infrastructure against emerging cyber threats.

The company raised €234 million, reaching unicorn status as it expands its approach to “Physical AI cybersecurity“.

Unlike traditional security solutions that protect networks from the outside, Exein embeds protection directly into devices and operating environments. Its runtime security technology continuously monitors system behaviour, detects suspicious activity and can block malicious actions before they execute.

Fleuret AI (France)

Founded in 2026, Fleuret AI is automating penetration testing with AI agents.

The Paris-based cybersecurity startup closed a €4 million pre-Seed round in October 2026 to hire AI, software engineering and offensive security talent, as well as accelerate platform development. By combining offensive security expertise with agentic AI, Fleuret is targeting more continuous and accessible penetration testing.

Hadrian (UK / Netherlands)

Founded in Amsterdam in 2021, Hadrian is building an agentic AI offensive security platform designed to continuously discover, validate and prioritise exposures across organisations’ digital attack surfaces.

In October 2026, the London-Amsterdam startup raised €35.68 million to expand across EMEA and the US, while deepening investment in engineering and research. Its platform sits at the intersection of offensive security, automation and AI-driven attack-surface management.

NeuralTrust (Spain)

Founded in 2022, Barcelona-based NeuralTrust focuses on protecting enterprise AI applications and autonomous agents against emerging security threats.

NeuralTrust’s platform monitors interactions between AI agents, users and connected tools, applying security controls in real time to detect and prevent potentially harmful behaviour.

In June 2026, the startup announced a €17.2 million Seed round, which is described as the largest cybersecurity Seed financing raised by an EU company to date.

As businesses increasingly rely on AI agents to access information and carry out tasks autonomously, NeuralTrust aims to help organisations prevent attackers from manipulating these systems or exploiting their access to sensitive enterprise environments.

Qevlar AI (France)

Founded in 2023, Paris-based Qevlar AI is using agentic AI to automate Security Operations Centre investigations.

The startup raised €25.8 million in March 2026 for its platform, which aims to support security teams by automating and deepening cyber investigations. As SOC (Security Operations Centre) teams face rising alert volumes and increasingly automated threats, Qevlar AI is positioning itself around faster, AI-assisted incident analysis.

QuoIntelligence (Germany)

Founded in 2020, Frankfurt-based QuoIntelligence provides EU-compliant threat intelligence, combining an AI-powered platform with human analysts.

The company closed a €7.3 million Series A in April 2026 to scale its work with organisations facing cyber risk, regulatory pressure and supply-chain oversight.

With European companies adapting to frameworks such as NIS2, which strengthens cybersecurity requirements across critical sectors, and DORA, which focuses on digital operational resilience in the financial sector, QuoIntelligence is focused on contextualised, sector-specific intelligence.

Trent AI (UK)

Founded in 2025, London-based Trent AI emerged from stealth in April 2026 with an €11 million Seed round to develop a layered cybersecurity platform built for the agentic era.

The startup is addressing the security challenges created by autonomous AI agents, which can interact with enterprise systems, access sensitive information and execute tasks with limited human supervision. These capabilities introduce new attack surfaces, including the potential misuse of permissions, compromised workflows and malicious manipulation of agent behaviour.

Zepo Intelligence (Spain)

Founded in 2021, Spain-based Zepo Intelligence is taking on AI-driven human-targeted cyber threats by enabling organisations to simulate real-world, AI-driven social engineering attacks such deepfakes, voice calls, cross-platform messages, or personalised phishing, and identify vulnerabilities

The startup raised €12.8 million in January of this year to protect workplaces from attacks such as impersonation, social engineering and other forms of human-layer compromise. Zepo Intelligence describes itself as an agentic social intelligence platform for workspace security.

In summary

Together, these companies show how Europe’s cybersecurity sector is evolving beyond traditional perimeter defence. The focus is not only on countering AI-powered cyberattacks, but also on securing autonomous AI agents, identifying vulnerabilities before they can be exploited, automating security operations and protecting the connected systems that increasingly underpin the digital economy.

“Great products usually come from people who’ve lived through the problem themselves. Content is basically free to produce now, but knowing what actually converts takes context and hands-on experience. Holo’s founders have both, and it’s what sets them apart. The company aims to automate marketing with its all-in-one platform. To get started, the business owner enters the company’s website. Holo learns what the business sells and how the brand looks and communicates, then uses that information, along with the owner’s goals, to suggest a marketing plan. 

The company says the plan covers which channels to use, what to launch on each, and what to skip, giving the owner a starting point without having to write a brief for every activity.

The platform carries that plan through to execution. It creates ads, social media posts, emails and SEO content in the business’s own voice, and organises them in a calendar. Holo notes that owners can review the proposed work, request changes, or approve it for publication across connected channels. An owner gets a plan built around their business, and that plan keeps changing based on what actually happened. This round lets us push that further, so more of the work can run on autopilot and the owner only steps in when they want to,” said Kovger, co-founder of Holo.

Holo uses third-party AI models, with its own technology built on top. The Lithuanian startup reported reaching $5 million in annual recurring revenue within 252 days, on less than €1 million raised before this round. More than 20,000 businesses across over 100 countries now pay for it.

“Most small business owners we talk to are great at what they do, and almost none of them started a business to do marketing. We think that within a few years a small business will be able to market the way the biggest brands do, with a real plan, constant testing and a clear decision every week about what to do next, and the owner won’t have to think about it any more than they think about how their bank processes payments. More than 20,000 businesses already pay for Holo, which tells us owners are ready for that, and this round is about getting them there faster,” says Urbanavicius, co-founder of Holo.

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><link rel="pingback" href="https://www.studyineurope.eu/xmlrpc.php"> <style id="sie-lean-layout"> #sie-lean-main { margin: 0; }
 #sie-lean-main > *:first-child,
 #sie-lean-main .sie-field-page { margin-top: 0; }
 .et_builder_inner_content { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_section { position: relative; }
 .et_pb_row { position: relative; width: 80%; max-width: 1080px; margin: 0 auto; }
 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {
 color: #ff6b6b !important;   /* slightly lighter red, readable on blue */
}
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link:hover {
 color: #ff4444 !important;
}
/* ── Responsive ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 :root {
 --sie-hdr-bar-h: 56px;
 }
 .sie-hdr {
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: flex;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav {
 /* Hidden off-screen when closed — no layout shift */
 position: absolute;
 top: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);           /* flush below the nav bar */
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter — same reason as .sie-hdr__bar */
 padding: 12px 0 20px;
 clip-path: inset(0 0 100% 0);       /* collapses upward — no CLS */
 transition: clip-path 0.3s ease;
 z-index: 9998;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav.is-open {
 clip-path: inset(0);
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list {
 flex-direction: column;
 align-items: flex-start;
 gap: 0;
 padding: 0 16px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__nav-list a,
 .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 width: 100%;
 font-size: 15px;
 padding: 12px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 position: static;
 box-shadow: none;
 border-radius: 0;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06);
 padding: 4px 0 4px 16px;
 margin: 4px 0;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);
 font-size: 14px;
 }
 .sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08);
 color: #fff;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 480px) {
 .sie-hdr__inner {
 padding: 0 16px;
 gap: 16px;
 }
}
/* Hover-gap fix: invisible bridge spanning the 6px gap between the nav item
 and the dropdown panel, so the cursor never "leaves" while crossing. */
.sie-hdr__dropdown::before {
 content: "";
 position: absolute;
 top: -10px;
 left: 0;
 right: 0;
 height: 10px;
}
/* Anti-FOUC guard for body-rendered overlays: their own CSS arrives 20KB+
 later in the HTML stream, so on slow connections they paint fully visible
 (the destinations grid "opens" during load). Force the CLOSED state from
 first paint — each component's .open/.is-open rules override these. */
.sie-dest-panel,
#sie-auth-drawer,
#sie-lead-form-drawer,
.sie-finder-overlay {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
} </style> <style id="sie-etmodules-font-display">@font-face{font-family:"ETmodules";src:url("https://www.studyineurope.eu/core/views/sie-theme/css/base/modules.woff") format("woff");font-style:normal;font-weight:normal;font-display:swap;}</style><meta name='robots' content='index, follow, max-image-preview:large, max-snippet:-1, max-video-preview:-1' /> <style id="sie-hide-divi-header"> /* Hide Divi's header (Theme Builder + classic) */

<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>

                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment. There should be individuals - such as mentors and counsellors - available to offer support.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides incoming mobile participants with access to the same services and facilities available to local students and staff</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Before the mobility, your institution has established formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to e.g. the use of Learning Agreements)</div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. Therefore, it is essential to conduct mobility based on an agreed and signed Learning Agreement. The Learning Agreement should be agreed and signed by all parties (the student, the sending institution and the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise) before the start of the mobility. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> At the end of the mobility, your institution has formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to recognition at the end of the mobility, e.g. in the use of Transcripts of Records and Grade Distribution Tables)</div>
